title: Hypsigenyinae — Hogfishes and Sheephead Wrasses
text:
Natural History
The Hypsigenyinae (hogfishes, sheephead wrasses, and tuskfishes) is a subfamily of Labridae comprising the genera Bodianus (~44 species), Choerodon (~25 species, tuskfishes), Semicossyphus (2 species, sheepheads), Clepticus (2 species, Creole wrasses), and several smaller genera. Your tree includes 38 species drawn from this clade. Molecular phylogenetics has revealed that Bodianus as traditionally defined is not monophyletic without the inclusion of Semicossyphus and Clepticus (Santini et al., 2016), and Gomon (2006) recognized 10 subgenera within Bodianus based on morphological characters. The first multi-locus time-calibrated phylogeny for the group placed the origin of the hogfish radiation in the Early Miocene, approximately 20 million years ago (Santini et al., 2016).
Hypsigenyines are hard-prey specialists. Bodianus species use their robust canine teeth to seize crabs, snails, sea urchins, and brittlestars, often carrying prey items to rock surfaces to crush them. Choerodon tuskfishes have taken this feeding specialization a step further: multiple species have been documented using rocks as anvils to break open bivalve shells — one of the best-documented examples of tool use in any fish (Jones et al., 2011; Bernardi, 2012). Choerodon schoenleinii on the Great Barrier Reef grasps a clam in its jaws, carries it to a favored anvil rock, and delivers alternating blows by rapidly rotating its body until the shell cracks. This cognitively complex behavior suggests that hypsigenyines may possess more sophisticated spatial cognition than is typical for reef fishes, an observation that connects intriguingly (if speculatively) to their often-elaborate coloration.
One of the most striking ecological features of this clade is its extraordinary depth range. While most reef fish families concentrate in the upper 30 m of the water column, hypsigenyines span from the intertidal zone (juvenile Semicossyphus pulcher, California sheephead, occurs in shallow tidepools) to well below 200 m (Bodianus species have been collected from deep rocky reefs and seamounts). This depth range is among the broadest of any labrid clade and provides a powerful natural experiment for testing how the ambient light environment shapes color evolution.
Reproductive biology follows the standard labrid pattern of protogynous hermaphroditism. A critical connection to color evolution is the cleaning behavior of juvenile Bodianus species. Many Bodianus juveniles serve as cleaner fish, adopting distinctive “cleaning livery” coloration — typically a bicolor pattern of dark upper body and pale lower body, often with a conspicuous lateral stripe — that advertises their cleaning services to larger reef fishes. This cleaning livery is lost during ontogeny as the fish transitions to the adult color pattern. The presence or absence of juvenile cleaning behavior and its associated livery is a tractable discrete trait for phylogenetic comparative analysis.
This is the smallest student group (2 students), with 38 species in the tree. While 38 species is adequate for most phylogenetic comparative methods, you should be aware that PGLS regressions and model-fitting procedures have reduced statistical power with smaller sample sizes. Focus on strong biological hypotheses and consider supplementing quantitative results with qualitative pattern descriptions.

title: Hypsigenyinae — Hogfishes and Sheephead Wrasses
text:
Color Pattern Diversity
Hypsigenyine coloration is diverse and often dramatic. Bodianus rufus (Spanish hogfish) displays a bold bicolor pattern: deep purple-blue anterior grading to bright yellow posterior. B. pulchellus (spotfin hogfish) shows vivid red-orange with white banding. Semicossyphus pulcher (California sheephead) undergoes one of the most extreme color transformations in the family: juveniles are bright orange-red with a white lateral stripe, females are uniform pink, and terminal-phase males are black head and tail with a broad red midbody band.
Tropical Bodianus species tend toward vivid reds, oranges, and yellows with contrasting dark markings, while temperate species (Semicossyphus, some deep-water Bodianus) are more often uniform pink, red, or dark reddish-brown. Choerodon tuskfishes display a different aesthetic: many are green, blue-green, or olive with complex facial markings and variable banding patterns.
The juvenile cleaning livery represents a distinct “color regime” that cuts across species boundaries. Juvenile cleaners in Bodianus typically show a dark dorsum and pale ventrum with a horizontal stripe — a pattern convergent with the juvenile livery of unrelated cleaner fishes (e.g., Labroides cleaner wrasses). This convergence across distantly related lineages is strong evidence that cleaning livery is shaped by client-fish recognition rather than phylogenetic inheritance.

title: Hypsigenyinae — Hogfishes and Sheephead Wrasses
text:
Dimorphism and Ontogeny Warnings






Data quality: what to watch for



IP/TP dimorphism — moderate but present. Hypsigenyines are protogynous hermaphrodites, and most species show some degree of IP/TP color difference. The dimorphism is typically less extreme than in Scarinae or Cirrhilabrini, but it is real:

Semicossyphus pulcher: TP males are unmistakable (black/red/black tricolor), while IPs (females) are uniform pink. Use TP males consistently.
Bodianus species: TP males tend to be more intensely colored with bolder markings. IP females are often similar in pattern but with muted colors. The difference is subtle enough in many species that either phase could be used, but be consistent within your dataset.
Choerodon: Dimorphism is variable. Some species show notable IP/TP differences (especially in facial markings), while others are nearly monomorphic.

Rule of thumb: Use TP male images when available. If you cannot determine sex from the image, use the most intensely colored individual available for each species.
Juvenile cleaning livery: Juvenile Bodianus with cleaning livery look dramatically different from adults. The bicolor pattern (dark dorsum / pale ventrum with lateral stripe) is a cleaning advertisement, not the species’ “real” color pattern for comparative purposes. Exclude cleaning-livery juveniles from your pavo analysis. They will cluster together in color space regardless of species identity, biasing your results.
How to recognize juvenile cleaners:

Small body size (typically < 5 cm).
Bold bicolor pattern: dark (black, brown, or deep blue) upper body and white or yellow lower body, often with a prominent horizontal stripe.
May be photographed near or on the body of a larger fish.

Small sample size: With 38 species, your statistical power for PGLS and model-comparison analyses is limited. Consider:

Using simpler models (BM vs. OU rather than multi-regime OU).
Emphasizing effect sizes and confidence intervals rather than p-values alone.
Supplementing quantitative analysis with qualitative pattern descriptions and phylogenetic trait mapping.

title: Hypsigenyinae — Hogfishes and Sheephead Wrasses
text:
Promising Questions for This Clade

Depth and Color — Hypsigenyinae has the broadest depth range of any student clade, spanning from the intertidal to beyond 200 m. This is arguably the single best group for testing the depth–color hypothesis. Do deep-dwelling species show reduced red/orange chroma and increased blue-shifted reflectance?
Discrete Trait Mapping — Map the presence/absence of juvenile cleaning livery onto the phylogeny. How many times has cleaning behavior (and its associated coloration) evolved in Bodianus? Is the cleaning livery pattern phylogenetically conserved or labile?
Body Size and Color Complexity — With body sizes ranging from small cleanerfish Bodianus (~10 cm) to the massive California sheephead (~90 cm), test whether larger species display different color metrics.
Cross-Family Comparison — Compare hypsigenyine color diversity to the other labrid clades (Scarinae, Cirrhilabrini, Halichoerine) to test whether the crusher feeding guild constrains color evolution relative to planktivores or herbivores.

title: Halichoerine — Coris-Allies and Halichoeres Wrasses
text:
Natural History
The Halichoerine clade is the largest group in the course, encompassing approximately 140 species drawn from some of the most species-rich genera within Labridae: Halichoeres (~83 species), Coris (~19 species), Thalassoma (~17 species), Macropharyngodon (~10 species), Anampses (~11 species), and several smaller genera. This clade represents the julidine lineage of wrasses — small to medium-sized, typically elongate reef fishes that are among the most abundant and conspicuous members of tropical reef communities worldwide. The phylogenomic analysis of Brownstein et al. (2025) confirmed that multiple lineages within this clade diversified rapidly during the Miocene, contributing to the explosive radiation of labrid diversity on coral reefs.
Halichoeres is the single largest wrasse genus and is circumtropically distributed across the Atlantic, Eastern Pacific, and Indo-Pacific. Molecular phylogenetics has revealed that Halichoeres as traditionally defined is likely polyphyletic — species currently placed in the genus may not all share a single common ancestor exclusive of other genera (Barber & Bellwood, 2005; Price et al., 2018). This means that patterns of color evolution mapped onto the Halichoeres phylogeny may reflect deep evolutionary divergences rather than recent radiation within a single lineage. The polyphyly of Halichoeres is itself an important finding for your analysis: it means that apparent “within-genus” color diversity may actually span multiple independent evolutionary lineages.
A defining biogeographic story in this clade involves geminate species pairs across the Isthmus of Panama. When the isthmus closed approximately 3 million years ago, it divided ancestral populations of marine species into Caribbean (Atlantic) and Eastern Pacific descendants. Halichoeres contains several well-documented geminate pairs: H. bivittatus (Atlantic) and H. dispilus (Pacific), H. maculipinna (Atlantic) and H. chierchiae (Pacific). Price et al. (2018) showed that five of 25 speciation events in New World Halichoeres occurred across this barrier, though not all at the time of final closure — some trans-Isthmian splits are much older (up to ~20 Ma). These geminate pairs offer a natural experiment: how much has color diverged between sister species separated by a well-dated vicariance event?
Ecologically, halichoerine wrasses are primarily invertivores, foraging on sand flats, rubble zones, and reef edges for small crustaceans, polychaetes, and mollusks. Several genera have distinctive foraging behaviors: Coris species dig through sand for buried invertebrates; Thalassoma species are fast-swimming generalists that also pick zooplankton from the water column; Macropharyngodon (“leopard wrasses”) specialize on small, hard-shelled invertebrates (foraminifera, ostracods) and have distinctive pharyngeal jaw dentition. One of the most widespread behaviors in the clade is sand-sleeping: many species bury themselves in sand at night or when threatened, a behavior that may impose constraints on coloration (sand-sleeping species may benefit from cryptic dorsal coloration visible from above).

title: Halichoerine — Coris-Allies and Halichoeres Wrasses
text:
Color Pattern Diversity
The halichoerine clade contains some of the most extreme color diversity in any single labrid lineage. Macropharyngodon leopard wrasses display intricate, almost psychedelic patterns of teal spots, orange rosettes, and irregular black outlines on a pale background — each individual has a unique pattern, like a fingerprint. Thalassoma species are characterized by bold facial stripes and head patterns: T. lunare (moon wrasse) has a green body with vivid magenta-to-yellow face markings, while T. bifasciatum (bluehead wrasse) is one of the most studied reef fishes in the world, with TP males displaying a brilliant blue head separated from a green body by black-and-white vertical bars. Coris gaimard undergoes dramatic ontogenetic color change: juveniles are bright orange-red with white-edged black dorsal spots (“clown” pattern), while adults develop a dark blue-green body with brilliant blue facial spots.
Halichoeres species span the full spectrum from drab to vivid. Some sand-associated species (e.g., H. poeyi, H. bivittatus IP) are olive-green or brown with subtle stripes and blotches, while others (e.g., H. ornatissimus, the ornate wrasse) display rainbow-like patterns of red, green, blue, and orange facial stripes. This genus-level color variation — from cryptic to maximally conspicuous — within a single (albeit polyphyletic) genus makes Halichoeres ideal for testing ecological predictors of color evolution.
Anampses wrasses show a different pattern: many species display intricate spotting and line patterns on a dark body, with dramatic IP/TP differences. A. meleagrides females are black with white spots, while TP males are dark green with blue facial lines and an orange tail.

title: Halichoerine — Coris-Allies and Halichoeres Wrasses
text:
Dimorphism and Ontogeny Warnings






Data quality: what to watch for



IP/TP dimorphism — present and important. Like all labrid clades, halichoerine wrasses are protogynous hermaphrodites with IP/TP color differences. The magnitude of dimorphism varies by genus:

Thalassoma: Strong dimorphism. TP males (e.g., bluehead wrasse blue phase) are dramatically different from IPs (yellow/brown). Use TP males.
Halichoeres: Moderate to strong dimorphism. TP males typically show more vivid colors and bolder markings than IPs. Use TP males.
Coris: Moderate dimorphism. TP males are generally more intensely colored with more defined facial patterns.
Macropharyngodon: Moderate dimorphism. Both phases are intricately patterned, but TP males tend toward more saturated colors and sharper pattern boundaries.
Anampses: Strong dimorphism. IP and TP can look like completely different species. Use TP males.

General rule: Use TP male images consistently. In labrids, females and juveniles often retain the juvenile color morph. If you cannot determine sex, choose the most vivid/boldly patterned individual, which is likely a TP male.
Ontogenetic changes: Coris species undergo dramatic juvenile-to-adult color transformation (e.g., C. gaimard juvenile “clown” pattern to adult blue-green). Thalassoma juveniles are typically uniformly colored (yellow, green, or brown) and lack the facial markings of adults. Exclude juveniles.
Dataset size management: With 140 species, this is by far the largest student dataset. Not all species will have high-quality photographs. Rather than including poor-quality or uncertain images for every species, focus on a well-sampled subset of 50–70 species that have:

Clear, high-resolution lateral-view photographs
Confirmed TP male individuals
Verified species identification

A well-curated subset of 60 species will produce more reliable pavo metrics than a noisy dataset of 140 species with mixed phases, poor images, and misidentifications. Document which species you excluded and why — this is good scientific practice, not a weakness.
Polyphyly of Halichoeres: Your tree may show Halichoeres species scattered across multiple parts of the phylogeny rather than forming a single clade. This is not a tree error — it reflects the genuine polyphyly of the genus. When reporting results, consider analyzing well-supported subclades of Halichoeres separately rather than treating the genus as a single unit.

title: Halichoerine — Coris-Allies and Halichoeres Wrasses
text:
Promising Questions for This Clade

Biogeographic Color Comparison — The geminate species pairs across the Isthmus of Panama provide a powerful natural experiment. Have Caribbean and Pacific sister species diverged in color metrics since vicariant separation? Is the magnitude of color divergence correlated with time since divergence?
Cross-Family Comparison — As the largest labrid clade in the course, halichoerine wrasses contribute the most species to the combined labrid mega-analysis. Compare the color morphospace occupied by your clade to the other three labrid groups (Scarinae, Cirrhilabrini, Hypsigenyinae). Does the largest clade occupy the broadest color space?
Phylogenetic Signal — With 140 species (or your curated subset), you have the best statistical power for estimating phylogenetic signal (Blomberg’s K, Pagel’s lambda). Is color more phylogenetically conserved in some genera (Macropharyngodon, with its distinctive spotted pattern) than others (Halichoeres, with its broad color range)?
Axis of Diversification — With extreme color diversity spanning from cryptic sand-dwellers to psychedelic leopard wrasses, which axis of pavo color space (brightness, saturation, hue, pattern complexity) shows the greatest disparity? Is the primary axis of color diversification the same across all genera?
Swimming Mode and Pattern — Halichoerine wrasses include both labriform swimmers (pectoral fin propulsion) and more body-undulatory swimmers. Does swimming mode correlate with stripe orientation or color pattern geometry?

title: Cirrhilabrini — Fairy Wrasses and Flasher Wrasses
text:
Natural History
The Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses and flasher wrasses) is a tribe within the family Labridae comprising the genera Cirrhilabrus (~60 species), Paracheilinus (~20 species), and several smaller allied genera. This is one of the most rapidly diversifying lineages of coral reef fishes: Tea et al. (2022) used phylogenomic analysis of 991 ultraconserved elements to demonstrate that Cirrhilabrus experienced explosive radiation recently, with many sister species diverging within the past 2–5 million years. This recent diversification, combined with the extraordinary importance of male coloration in species recognition and mate choice, makes Cirrhilabrini one of the most compelling systems in the ocean for studying the role of sexual selection in color diversification.
Cirrhilabrines are planktivorous fishes that hover in loose aggregations above reef substrate, feeding on small zooplankton carried by currents. Most species are associated with reef slopes, rubble zones, or deepwater reef edges. Several lineages have independently colonized mesophotic coral ecosystems (MCEs) at depths of 40–150 m, where light conditions are dramatically different from shallow reefs. These mesophotic specialists often display reduced red and orange coloration and increased emphasis on blue, violet, and UV-reflective patterns — adaptations that align with the spectral properties of ambient light at depth. This depth gradient offers a natural experiment for testing how the light environment constrains color evolution.
The taxonomy of Cirrhilabrini is among the most active frontiers in reef fish systematics. Numerous new species have been described since 2015, often from mesophotic habitats or geographically restricted localities. Cirrhilabrus finifenmaa (Tea et al., 2022) was described from the Maldives based on morphological, molecular, and coloration data — the species had been confused with C. rubrisquamis for decades. Many undescribed species likely remain, particularly in the Indo-Pacific archipelagos and deeper reef habitats. This taxonomic dynamism means that some species in your tree may have been recently split, synonymized, or reclassified since the tree was published.
Reproduction is driven by intense sexual selection. Males are protogynous hermaphrodites that maintain small harems on reef slopes. During courtship, males perform a “nuptial flash” display: they rapidly ascend above the reef, extend their fins to maximum spread, and undergo a dramatic, instantaneous intensification of body coloration — reds become incandescent, blues fluoresce, and pattern elements that are subtle during resting coloration become boldly defined. This flashing display lasts only seconds and may be repeated dozens of times during a courtship bout. The nuptial flash is the most extreme example of rapid color change in any reef fish group and represents the primary axis of sexual selection in this clade.
crumbs: Cirrhilabrini --- Fairy Wrasses and Flasher Wrasses

title: Cirrhilabrini — Fairy Wrasses and Flasher Wrasses
text:
Color Pattern Diversity
Male cirrhilabrine coloration spans a remarkable spectrum. Cirrhilabrus jordani (Hawaiian flame wrasse) displays brilliant orange-red during nuptial display; C. cyanopleura shows vivid blue and purple with a yellow-green saddle; C. temminckii combines magenta fins with a green-blue body. Paracheilinus flasher wrasses are named for their even more dramatic fin extensions during display, with P. nursalim showing electric blue dorsal fin filaments against a red body.
An extraordinary feature of this clade is the convergent drab coloration of females. Across almost all Cirrhilabrus and Paracheilinus species, females are small (typically 4–6 cm), uniformly pinkish-tan to mauve, with at most a faint lateral stripe or subtle fin tinting. This convergent female coloration is so extreme that females of different species are often impossible to distinguish in the field — or even from photographs. This pattern strongly suggests that female coloration is under stabilizing selection (crypsis from predators), while male coloration is under directional sexual selection (species recognition and mate attraction).
Color convergences across families are less pronounced than in other clades, because cirrhilabrine coloration is largely driven by sexual selection rather than ecological factors. However, the nuptial color intensification phenomenon has parallels in some damselfishes (Pomacentridae) and dottybacks (Pseudochromidae).

title: Cirrhilabrini — Fairy Wrasses and Flasher Wrasses
text:
Dimorphism and Ontogeny Warnings






Data quality: what to watch for



Extreme sexual dimorphism — use TP males. Like parrotfishes, cirrhilabrines have extreme dimorphism, but the pattern is different. In Scarinae, the issue is that IP and TP look like different species. In Cirrhilabrini, the issue is that females of different species look nearly identical, while males are the highly differentiated phase. Your analysis should use male (TP) images consistently.
How to identify males:

Color: Vivid, species-specific patterns with bold reds, blues, purples, greens, or combinations. Complex fin markings, often with elongated or filamentous dorsal rays.
Size: Males are generally larger than females within a species (6–10 cm for most Cirrhilabrus).
Behavior (in photos): Males are often photographed displaying (fins spread, body angled upward).

How to identify females (to exclude or flag):

Color: Uniform pinkish-tan, mauve, or light reddish-brown. Minimal fin coloration. May have a faint lateral stripe.
Size: Smaller, more streamlined.
If you cannot determine whether an image is a male or female, it is almost certainly a female — males are unmistakable.

Nuptial vs. resting coloration: Male Cirrhilabrus and Paracheilinus show two distinct color states: a muted “resting” coloration and an intensified “nuptial flash” coloration. Most underwater photographs capture resting coloration. Aquarium photographs sometimes capture nuptial display. For consistency, use resting-state male images across all species. If you only have nuptial-display images for some species and resting images for others, your color metrics will be biased.
Identical-looking females are real biology, not a data problem. When you see that your female images for 15 different species look essentially the same, do not assume you have misidentified species. This convergent female coloration is a genuine evolutionary phenomenon and is itself an interesting finding worth discussing in your analysis.
Recent taxonomic changes: Some species in your tree may have been split or renamed since 2022. Cross-check any unfamiliar names against the original Tea et al. (2022) phylogeny and current FishBase/Catalog of Fishes records.
crumbs: Cirrhilabrini --- Fairy Wrasses and Flasher Wrasses

title: Cirrhilabrini — Fairy Wrasses and Flasher Wrasses
text:
Promising Questions for This Clade

Sexual System and Color Complexity — Cirrhilabrini is the ultimate test case for sexual selection driving color diversification. Is male conspicuousness (measured by pavo metrics like Jc, Jt, or dS) correlated with proxies for mating system intensity? Do species with more elaborate fin extensions also show greater color complexity?
Disparity Through Time — With rapid recent diversification documented by Tea et al. (2022), cirrhilabrines are ideal for DTT analysis. Has male color diversified faster than expected under Brownian motion? Has the rate of color evolution accelerated during the recent species radiation?
Depth and Color — Multiple cirrhilabrine lineages have independently invaded mesophotic reefs. Do mesophotic specialists show predictable shifts in color metrics (e.g., reduced red chroma, increased short-wavelength reflectance) compared to shallow-reef relatives?
Phylogenetic Signal — Given that male coloration is the primary species-recognition signal, do you expect strong or weak phylogenetic signal in male color metrics? If sexual selection drives rapid divergence, signal may be low despite the clade’s youth.

title: Pomacanthidae — Marine Angelfishes
text:
Natural History
The Pomacanthidae (marine angelfishes) comprise approximately 90 species in 8 genera, distributed across tropical and subtropical reefs of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific oceans. The family is divided into two major ecological groups: the large-bodied angelfishes (Pomacanthus, Holacanthus, Chaetodontoplus) and the pygmy or dwarf angelfishes (Centropyge and allies). Your tree includes 56 species, but also contains several outgroup taxa from other families used for phylogenetic context (see warning below). Molecular phylogenetics has revealed that Centropyge as traditionally defined is paraphyletic — the genera Apolemichthys and Genicanthus nest within it (Gaither et al., 2014). This taxonomic instability is itself an interesting color-evolution story: species that look dramatically different in coloration turn out to be close relatives, while species that look nearly identical can be genetically distinct.
Angelfishes are characteristic members of coral reef communities, occupying territories on reef slopes, walls, and lagoon patch reefs. Large-bodied species are primarily spongivores, supplementing their diet with tunicates, algae, and small invertebrates. Pygmy angelfishes tend toward omnivory, grazing on algae and detrital films while also consuming small benthic invertebrates. Most species form harems in which a dominant male defends a territory containing several smaller females. Upon the death or removal of the male, the largest female undergoes sex change (protogynous hermaphroditism) — a process that is typically accompanied by a color change, sometimes dramatic. The tight coupling between social status, sex, and coloration makes pomacanthids a compelling system for studying the co-evolution of sexual and social signals.
Pomacanthids are perhaps most famous for their extreme ontogenetic color change. Juvenile emperor angelfish (Pomacanthus imperator) display electric blue and white concentric rings on a dark navy body — a pattern that provides camouflage among coral rubble and may reduce aggression from territorial adults. As the fish matures (at approximately 8–12 cm body length), the concentric rings gradually elongate and fade, transforming over several months into the adult pattern of alternating horizontal blue and yellow stripes. This transformation is so complete that early taxonomists described the juveniles and adults as separate species. Similar but distinct ontogenetic shifts occur in P. semicirculatus, P. annularis, and many other large-bodied pomacanthids. This extreme ontogenetic color change makes angelfishes one of the best study systems for understanding the developmental regulation and evolutionary lability of color pattern.
Hybridization is remarkably common in Pomacanthidae, particularly among Centropyge species. The family has the highest proportion of documented hybrids of any coral reef fish family. Hybrid individuals often display intermediate color patterns, creating a “color continuum” between parent species that has caused persistent taxonomic confusion and has implications for how we interpret discrete color categories in comparative analyses.

title: Pomacanthidae — Marine Angelfishes
text:
Color Pattern Diversity
Pomacanthids display a spectacular range of color patterns. At one extreme, Centropyge pygmy angelfishes include species that are almost entirely a single vivid color — the flame angelfish (C. loricula) is bright orange-red with black vertical bars, while the lemonpeel angelfish (C. flavissima) is uniformly bright yellow with a blue eye-ring. At the other extreme, large Pomacanthus species display complex multicolor patterns: the regal angelfish (Pygoplites diacanthus) has alternating yellow and blue-edged white vertical bars on a blue background.
Sexual dichromatism is most pronounced in Genicanthus (swallowtail angelfishes), where males and females can differ dramatically: male G. lamarck has bold horizontal black stripes on a white body, while females show a dark upper body fading to white below. In most other genera, dichromatism is subtle to moderate.
Color convergences across families are notable. The bold vertical barring of many angelfishes is paralleled in butterflyfishes (Chaetodontidae), which occupy similar reef habitats. The juvenile concentric-ring pattern of Pomacanthus has no close parallel in other reef fish families, making it a genuinely unique developmental phenomenon.

title: Pomacanthidae — Marine Angelfishes
text:
Dimorphism and Ontogeny Warnings






Data quality: what to watch for



Outgroup taxa in your tree: Your phylogeny includes species from outside Pomacanthidae that were used as outgroups in the original phylogenetic analysis. Expect to see tip labels for Chaetodon (butterflyfishes), Forcipiger (longnose butterflyfishes), Naso (unicornfishes), Zanclus (Moorish idol), and Acanthurus (surgeonfishes). You must exclude these outgroup taxa from your color-pattern analyses. They are there to root the tree, not to be part of your pomacanthid dataset. Filter them out before computing any pavo summary statistics.
Ontogenetic color change: This is the single biggest data-quality risk for your group. Juvenile and adult Pomacanthus and Holacanthus look like entirely different species. If your image set includes photographs of juvenile angelfish, they will introduce massive noise into your analysis. When curating images:

Verify that each image is an adult (or sub-adult with predominantly adult pattern).
Juveniles of Pomacanthus are characterized by concentric rings, spots, or bars on a dark body.
When in doubt, check body size relative to known adult size for the species. If the fish appears to be less than half the species’ maximum total length, treat it as a juvenile.

Dimorphism: Outside of Genicanthus, sexual dimorphism is moderate and often involves subtle differences in fin coloration or body saturation rather than wholesale pattern changes. For most genera, a single representative image per species is adequate. For Genicanthus, you may want to note whether you are using male or female images and be consistent.
Hybridization: Centropyge hybrids are common and often display intermediate coloration that does not match either parent species. If a specimen looks “off” relative to standard field guides, it may be a hybrid. Flag these for review rather than forcing them into a species category.

title: Pomacanthidae — Marine Angelfishes
text:
Promising Questions for This Clade

Discrete Trait Mapping — Map the juvenile-to-adult pattern transformation across the pomacanthid phylogeny. Is extreme ontogenetic color change ancestral to the family, or has it evolved independently in multiple lineages? Do pygmy angelfishes (Centropyge), which show less dramatic ontogenetic change, represent the derived condition?
Depth and Color — Pomacanthids range from shallow lagoons to deeper reef slopes, with some Centropyge and Paracentropyge occurring in mesophotic zones below 50 m. Do deeper-dwelling species show reduced conspicuousness, as predicted by the depth–color hypothesis?
Evolutionary Model Comparison — Given the paraphyly of Centropyge and the prevalence of hybridization, pomacanthids may violate the assumptions of standard Brownian motion models. Test whether Ornstein-Uhlenbeck models with multiple optima better fit your color data.
Cross-Family Comparison — Angelfishes are often confused with butterflyfishes by casual observers, and several species share convergent color patterns (vertical bars, eyespots, bold contrasts). A formal comparison of color metrics between Pomacanthidae and the outgroup Chaetodon species in your tree could test whether this convergence is quantitatively real.

title: Acanthuridae — Surgeonfishes, Tangs, and Unicornfishes
text:
Natural History
The Acanthuridae (surgeonfishes, tangs, and unicornfishes) is a family of approximately 86 species in 6 genera, distributed across tropical and subtropical reefs worldwide. The family is characterized by the caudal peduncle spine (or “scalpel”) — a sharp, blade-like structure at the base of the tail that can be erected during defensive or agonistic encounters. In many species, this spine is brightly colored (yellow, orange, or white against a dark body), making it a candidate for aposematic signaling. The caudal scalpel is a genuine weapon: it can inflict deep lacerations on predators, competitors, and careless divers, and its presence distinguishes acanthurids from all other reef fish families. This combination of a real defense with a conspicuous marking makes surgeonfishes uniquely suited for testing the link between weaponry and color evolution.
The three major genera structure acanthurid diversity: Acanthurus (~40 species, typical surgeonfishes), Naso (~20 species, unicornfishes), and Ctenochaetus (~10 species, bristletooth surgeonfishes). These genera occupy distinct feeding niches: most Acanthurus are grazing herbivores that crop algal turfs from reef substrate; Ctenochaetus species are detritivores that use comb-like teeth to sweep fine organic particles from surfaces; and Naso includes both grazers and open-water planktivores that form large midwater aggregations. The smaller genera Zebrasoma (tangs), Paracanthurus, and Prionurus round out the family. This diversity of feeding guilds within a single family provides a strong ecological axis for color-pattern analysis.
Surgeonfishes are broadcast spawners, typically releasing gametes during pair or group spawning rushes at reef edges during outgoing tides. Unlike labrids, most acanthurids are gonochoristic — they do not change sex — and sexual dichromatism is weak to absent in most species. Some species show transient courtship color changes: males of Acanthurus nigricans temporarily pale their body during spawning rushes, and A. lineatus males intensify the contrast of their facial stripes during territorial displays. These context-dependent color changes, while not as dramatic as labrid nuptial displays, add complexity to the interpretation of color metrics from static photographs.
This is the walkthrough dataset for the course. Frédérich et al. (2026) used Acanthuridae as one of six focal families in their global analysis of color pattern evolution in reef fishes, coding 30 pattern types across 918 species from six families. Your group’s analysis will follow a similar approach but with pavo-derived quantitative metrics.

title: Acanthuridae — Surgeonfishes, Tangs, and Unicornfishes
text:
Color Pattern Diversity
Acanthurid coloration ranges from uniform and relatively drab to strikingly bold. At one extreme, Ctenochaetus strigosus is uniformly brown with fine dark streaks, while at the other, Acanthurus lineatus displays brilliant alternating blue-and-orange horizontal stripes. Zebrasoma flavescens (the yellow tang) is uniformly bright yellow — one of the most recognizable reef fish in the world — while its congener Z. veliferum has complex brown-and-yellow vertical barring with extended dorsal and anal fins.
Unicornfishes (Naso) present a distinctive morphology: several species develop a prominent rostral horn and display muted blue-gray or olive body coloration with brightly colored caudal peduncle spines (paired in Naso, unlike the single retractable scalpel in Acanthurus). The coloration of the scalpel region is often the most conspicuous element of the fish and may serve a dual function: warning potential aggressors and facilitating species recognition in mixed-species feeding aggregations.
One of the most remarkable color stories in Acanthuridae involves Batesian mimicry. Juvenile Acanthurus pyroferus (the mimic surgeonfish) adopt the color pattern of locally common pygmy angelfishes (Centropyge spp.), including C. vrolikii, C. flavissima, C. heraldi, and C. eibli, depending on which model species is present in their habitat. As adults, A. pyroferus transitions to a uniform chocolate-brown coloration, losing all resemblance to its angelfish models. This ontogenetic mimicry system — mimicking different models in different geographic locations — is one of the most sophisticated examples of color-based deception on coral reefs.
Several species also show rapid context-dependent color change. Paracanthurus hepatus (blue tang) can pale its blue coloration dramatically when stressed, and several Acanthurus species temporarily display a pale bar or spot pattern during cleaning interactions or submissive encounters.

title: Acanthuridae — Surgeonfishes, Tangs, and Unicornfishes
text:
Dimorphism and Ontogeny Warnings






Data quality: what to watch for



Weak dichromatism — simpler data curation. Unlike labrids and scarines, most acanthurids show little or no sexual dimorphism in coloration. Males and females of the same species look essentially identical in photographs. This means a single representative image per species is generally adequate, and you do not need to worry about IP/TP confusion.
Context-dependent color change: Some species can temporarily alter their color in response to stress, social context, or cleaning interactions. Images taken of stressed fish (netted, recently captured, or in poor aquarium conditions) may show washed-out or abnormally pale coloration that does not represent the species’ typical appearance. When curating images:

Prefer photographs of undisturbed fish in natural reef settings.
Avoid images where the fish appears unusually pale, mottled, or shows a “fright pattern.”
If you have multiple images of the same species, select the one that best represents the species’ typical daytime reef coloration.

Juvenile mimicry in A. pyroferus: If your image set includes juvenile A. pyroferus, they will look like Centropyge angelfishes, not surgeonfishes. Use only adult images for this species (uniform chocolate-brown with a yellow eye-patch).
Ontogeny in other species: Most acanthurid juveniles resemble adults in pattern, though colors may be less saturated. The “acronurus” larval stage (transparent, disc-shaped, pelagic) will not appear in your image set. Juvenile Naso species lack the rostral horn and caudal spine development of adults but share similar body coloration.
Species identification: Several Acanthurus species are superficially similar (e.g., A. nigricans vs. A. achilles vs. A. japonicus). Pay attention to caudal spine coloration and facial markings for accurate identification.

title: Acanthuridae — Surgeonfishes, Tangs, and Unicornfishes
text:
Promising Questions for This Clade

Functional Hypothesis Testing — Surgeonfishes have a genuine weapon (the caudal scalpel) that makes aposematism biologically plausible. Test whether species with more conspicuously colored scalpels (bright yellow/orange against dark body) show higher overall body conspicuousness, as predicted by honest signaling of defensive capability.
Diet and Conspicuousness — With three distinct feeding guilds (grazing, detritivory, planktivory), acanthurids offer a clean test of the prediction that feeding ecology shapes color evolution. Are planktivorous species (which are exposed in the water column) more or less conspicuous than benthic grazers?
Cross-Family Comparison — As the walkthrough dataset, your pavo metrics can be directly compared to other clades. How does the overall color diversity (morphospace volume) of Acanthuridae compare to similarly sized labrid clades?
Discrete Trait Mapping — Map mimicry (juvenile A. pyroferus mimicking Centropyge), scalpel coloration (bright vs. cryptic), and the presence of horizontal striping across the phylogeny to test how many times each trait has evolved.
Latitude Gradient — Several acanthurid species extend into subtropical or warm-temperate waters. Test whether higher-latitude species show reduced conspicuousness compared to tropical congeners.

title: Scarinae — Parrotfishes
text:
Natural History
Parrotfishes (subfamily Scarinae) are a clade of approximately 100 species nested within the family Labridae. Their evolutionary history has been shaped by two defining innovations: the fused beak-like oral jaws that give them their common name, and the pharyngeal mill — a set of interlocking pharyngeal jaw plates that grind ingested reef substrate into fine sedite. These feeding adaptations have made parrotfishes the dominant agents of bioerosion on coral reefs worldwide, contributing tons of sediment per hectare per year to reef sand budgets. The phylogenetic position of Scarinae within Labridae was established by molecular data (Streelman et al., 2002; Westneat & Alfaro, 2005) and confirmed by the comprehensive phylogenomic analysis of Brownstein et al. (2025), which placed the parrotfish radiation within the broader context of labrid diversification during the Miocene.
Two major functional groups structure parrotfish feeding ecology: scrapers (e.g., Scarus, most Sparisoma) that remove a thin layer of substrate with their beaks, and excavators (e.g., Chlorurus, Bolbometopon) that gouge deep chunks from the reef framework. Scraping vs. excavating has evolved recurrently across the scarinine phylogeny and correlates with jaw morphology, body size, and habitat use (Bellwood, 1994; Streelman et al., 2002). This functional divergence provides a strong ecological axis for color-pattern analysis.
A deep biogeographic split divides the parrotfishes: the Atlantic genus Sparisoma (~15 species) diverged early from the Indo-Pacific radiation that includes Scarus (~50 species), Chlorurus (~17 species), and Bolbometopon (1 species). Atlantic Sparisoma tend to retain more of the ancestral red-brown coloration, while Indo-Pacific Scarus and Chlorurus have diversified into vivid blues, greens, and complex multicolor patterns. This Atlantic vs. Indo-Pacific split is one of the cleanest natural experiments in reef fish color evolution.
The reproductive biology of parrotfishes is dominated by protogynous hermaphroditism, typically in a diandric system: some individuals begin life as females and later undergo sex change to become terminal-phase (TP) males, while others are born as primary males that initially resemble females (initial phase, IP). Sex change is accompanied by a dramatic color transformation — arguably the most extreme in any vertebrate group. This creates the IP/TP dimorphism that defines the data challenges (and opportunities) for your group.

title: Scarinae — Parrotfishes
text:
Color Pattern Diversity
Parrotfish color diversity is overwhelmingly structured by the IP/TP dimorphism. Initial-phase individuals (females and primary males) are typically drab: muted red-brown, olive, or gray, often with irregular darker blotching. Terminal-phase males, by contrast, are spectacularly colored: vivid blue-green heads, complex facial patterns with pink, orange, or teal markings, and body coloration ranging from emerald to turquoise to deep blue. The contrast between IP and TP in a single species can be so extreme that early taxonomists routinely described them as separate species — Scarus vetula and S. guacamaia IP and TP forms were classified under different names for decades.
Within the TP color space, there is substantial interspecific variation. Scarus quoyi TP males are deep blue-green with a pink lower jaw; Chlorurus microrhinos TPs are bright green with a prominent cephalic hump; Bolbometopon muricatum TPs are olive-gray with a massive forehead bump. Sparisoma viride shows a more moderate dimorphism, with TPs displaying dark green bodies and crescent-shaped tail markings, and IPs showing red-brown bodies with a white spot at the caudal peduncle.
Size variation is also remarkable: the cryptic, cigar-shaped Cryptotomus roseus reaches only ~12 cm total length, while the bumphead parrotfish Bolbometopon muricatum exceeds 130 cm and 46 kg — a body size range of more than 10-fold within a single subfamily.

title: Scarinae — Parrotfishes
text:
Dimorphism and Ontogeny Warnings






Data quality: THIS IS YOUR BIGGEST CHALLENGE



IP/TP dimorphism — use TP males consistently. This is the single most important data-quality issue for your group. Initial-phase and terminal-phase parrotfishes look like entirely different species. If you mix IP and TP images in your pavo analysis, your color metrics will be meaningless. Use only TP (terminal-phase) male images for your comparative analysis.
How to identify TP males:

Color: Vivid blues, greens, teals, with complex facial markings (lines, swirls, spots around the eye and jaw).
Body shape: In many species, TP males are larger and may develop a cephalic hump (especially Chlorurus, Bolbometopon).
Behavior (in photos): TP males are often photographed solo or patrolling a territory, while IP individuals often appear in loose groups.

How to identify IP individuals (to exclude):

Color: Drab red-brown, olive, gray, or muted maroon. May have irregular blotches or a more uniform, washed-out appearance.
Body shape: Smaller, no cephalic hump, more streamlined.

Juveniles: Very young parrotfish may show yet another color pattern. Juvenile Scarus are often uniformly dark brown or gray, sometimes with a pale stripe. In labrids including scarines, females and juveniles often retain the juvenile color morph. You will encounter some juvenile images in your set — exclude them.
Species-specific notes:

Sparisoma species: IP/TP dimorphism is less extreme than in Scarus/Chlorurus. IPs still tend toward red-brown, TPs toward green/blue, but the difference is subtler.
Cryptotomus roseus: Minimal dimorphism; both phases are translucent pink. This species will be an outlier in your color space.
Bolbometopon muricatum: Adults are relatively uniform olive-gray regardless of phase. TP males are identified by their massive size and prominent forehead bump rather than color.

Consistency rule: For every species in your analysis, verify that you are using a TP male image. If a TP male image is not available for a given species, it is better to exclude that species than to use an IP image and introduce noise.

title: Scarinae — Parrotfishes
text:
Promising Questions for This Clade

Sexual System and Color Complexity — Scarinae is the ideal clade for testing whether protogynous hermaphroditism drives the evolution of extreme dichromatism. Compare TP male conspicuousness across species and ask whether the magnitude of IP–TP color difference correlates with mating system intensity (haremic vs. group spawning).
Body Size and Color Complexity — With a 10-fold size range from Cryptotomus to Bolbometopon, parrotfishes offer a strong gradient for testing whether larger species can “afford” more complex color patterns (greater visual target area, reduced predation risk).
Biogeographic Color Comparison — The Atlantic (Sparisoma) vs. Indo-Pacific (Scarus, Chlorurus) split is one of the cleanest biogeographic contrasts available. Do Indo-Pacific parrotfishes occupy a broader region of color space? Has the Atlantic lineage been more constrained in its color evolution?
Diet and Conspicuousness — Scrapers vs. excavators differ in feeding posture and reef-surface exposure time. Do excavators (which spend more time head-down on the reef face) differ in conspicuousness from scrapers?

title: Balistoidea — Triggerfishes and Filefishes
text:
Natural History
Balistoidea is the superfamily uniting the triggerfishes (Balistidae, ~40 species) and filefishes (Monacanthidae, ~100+ species). These two families are sister groups within the order Tetraodontiformes and diverged from each other during the Middle Eocene, roughly 45 million years ago. Crown-group filefishes are substantially older than crown-group triggerfishes, which helps explain why Monacanthidae is more than twice as species-rich as Balistidae despite similar rates of speciation and body-size evolution (Santini et al., 2013). The modern balistid radiation began in the Late Miocene, coinciding with reorganization of coral reef communities. This deep phylogenetic split — one ancient, species-rich clade and one younger, less diverse clade — makes balistoideans an excellent system for asking how evolutionary age versus ecological opportunity drives color pattern diversity.
Both families are broadly distributed across tropical and temperate oceans, though triggerfishes are most diverse on Indo-Pacific coral reefs while filefishes have also radiated into temperate and pelagic habitats. Triggerfishes are conspicuous, territorial reef dwellers that use their first dorsal spine as a locking mechanism for refuge in crevices. Filefishes are more morphologically and ecologically diverse, ranging from reef-associated species to oceanic forms like the oceanic filefish (Cantherhines pullus). Diet spans an extraordinary range: Balistapus undulatus crushes sea urchins with powerful jaws, Melichthys niger picks zooplankton from the water column, and Oxymonacanthus longirostris feeds almost exclusively on Acropora coral polyps. This dietary breadth is one of the most compelling ecological axes for predicting color patterns.
Reproductive behavior in balistoids is relatively simple compared to labrids: most species are gonochoristic (separate sexes throughout life) and many triggerfishes are territorial nest-guarders. Males of some triggerfish species (e.g., Rhinecanthus aculeatus) show subtle but measurable color differences during courtship, including darkening of the chin and intensification of facial stripes. Filefishes tend to show weaker behavioral color signaling, with a few notable exceptions such as the tasselled filefish (Chaetodermis penicilligerus), whose elaborate skin flaps and mottled coloration serve as camouflage rather than sexual advertisement. The generally weak dichromatism makes balistoids a good contrast case to the extreme dichromatism seen in labrid clades.
One of the most striking biological stories in this clade is the Batesian mimicry between the blacksaddle filefish Paraluteres prionurus and the highly toxic sharpnose pufferfish Canthigaster valentini. The filefish has evolved nearly identical coloration — four dark saddles on a white-yellow body — despite lacking the pufferfish’s tetrodotoxin. This mimicry system only works where the toxic model is common, and it represents one of the best-documented cases of interspecific color convergence on coral reefs. The presence of this mimicry system makes balistoideans uniquely suited for questions about convergent color evolution driven by predator-mediated selection.

title: Balistoidea — Triggerfishes and Filefishes
text:
Color Pattern Diversity
Balistoid color patterns span an impressive range. Triggerfishes include some of the most recognizable reef fish: the Picasso triggerfish (Rhinecanthus aculeatus) with its geometric facial stripes, the clown triggerfish (Balistoides conspicillum) with its bold white polka dots, and the redtooth triggerfish (Odonus niger) with its uniform dark blue-black. Filefishes tend toward more muted, cryptic coloration — many are brown, gray, or green with fine spotting or mottling that helps them blend into reef rubble or algae-covered substrates.
Several filefishes have evolved remarkable crypsis. Chaetodermis penicilligerus carries elaborate skin tassels that mimic algal growth, while Acreichthys tomentosus can adjust its mottled pattern to match different substrates. At the other extreme, some trigger species like Balistapus undulatus display vivid greens, oranges, and diagonal facial stripes that may serve as species recognition signals in multispecies reef assemblages.
Convergences with other families are notable. The bright facial patterning in Rhinecanthus is reminiscent of butterflyfish eyespots and facial stripes — patterns that Alfaro et al. (2019) showed evolve rapidly across Chaetodontidae. The mimicry of Paraluteres / Canthigaster crosses family and even ordinal boundaries (Tetraodontiformes to Tetraodontiformes, but Monacanthidae to Tetraodontidae).

title: Balistoidea — Triggerfishes and Filefishes
text:
Dimorphism and Ontogeny Warnings






Data quality: what to watch for



Dimorphism: Sexual dimorphism in balistoids is generally weak. Most species show no externally distinguishable sex differences in coloration, which simplifies your image curation. A few triggerfishes show subtle courtship-specific color changes (temporary darkening or stripe intensification in males), but these are ephemeral and unlikely to appear in your photograph set.
Ontogeny: Juvenile balistoids generally resemble adults in overall pattern, though colors may be muted and fine details less developed. Juvenile triggerfishes are occasionally more uniformly colored (lacking the full intensity of adult pattern elements), but the transformation is gradual rather than the dramatic metamorphosis seen in pomacanthids. You should still note specimen size when possible, as very small juveniles may lack diagnostic markings.
Taxonomy: Some species in your tree may appear under older synonyms on FishBase and in the primary literature. The family Monacanthidae is sometimes listed under alternative arrangements. Cross-check any species that does not immediately match by searching for its current accepted name in FishBase or the Catalog of Fishes.

title: Balistoidea — Triggerfishes and Filefishes
text:
Promising Questions for This Clade

Functional Hypothesis Testing — Triggerfishes have a locked first dorsal spine that makes them difficult to extract from crevices, a genuine anti-predator defense. Does the presence of this spine correlate with bolder, more conspicuous coloration (as predicted by aposematism theory)? Compare conspicuousness between triggerfishes (spined) and filefishes (spined but with a weaker locking mechanism).
Biogeographic Color Comparison — Balistoids include both tropical reef specialists and temperate-water species. Do tropical species show greater color diversity or conspicuousness than temperate relatives? The mix of biogeographic regions in your tree makes this comparison tractable.
Discrete Trait Mapping — Map the presence/absence of the Paraluteres/Canthigaster mimicry coloration onto the phylogeny. Has mimetic coloration evolved once or multiple times within Monacanthidae? Does the mimicry pattern cluster phylogenetically or appear convergently?
Diet and Conspicuousness — With diets ranging from planktivory to hard-prey crushing to obligate corallivory, balistoids offer a strong gradient for testing the prediction that diet-related exposure to predators shapes color evolution.
