title: Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison
text: Beyond drift, constraint, and early burst — does color evolve punctuationally, with a directional trend, or under an alternative mode?

title: Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison
text: Beyond drift, constraint, and early burst — does color evolve punctuationally, with a directional trend, or under an alternative mode?

title: Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Extended model selection for trait evolution



Recipe 20 tests three evolutionary models (BM, OU, EB). This recipe extends that comparison to eight models by adding Pagel’s branch-length transformations (lambda, kappa, delta), a directional trend model, and a white noise null. Each additional model captures a distinct evolutionary scenario that BM/OU/EB cannot distinguish. Together, the eight models cover nearly every major hypothesis about how a continuous trait might evolve on a phylogeny.

title: Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Recipe 20 may tell you that BM wins — but what if the real process is punctuational change concentrated at speciation events (kappa), or a directional trend toward increasing color complexity over time? These alternatives are invisible to a BM/OU/EB comparison. By fitting all eight models, you cast a wider net and reduce the chance of missing the true evolutionary mode. If kappa wins, your story becomes about speciation-associated change. If delta wins, you learn whether evolution was front-loaded or back-loaded. If lambda wins with a low value, phylogeny may not predict color at all.






Clade-specific tips




Pomacanthidae (angelfishes): If kappa < 1 wins, color changes at speciation events rather than along branches — consistent with the dramatic genus-level color differences in angelfishes.
Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): A trend model might capture directional evolution toward increasing male display color complexity, driven by persistent sexual selection.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): Delta < 1 (early change) would be consistent with the deep split between the two families establishing distinct color strategies early.
Scarinae (parrotfishes): The lambda model might reveal that phylogenetic signal in color is weaker than the tree topology suggests, because phase changes scramble the phylogenetic pattern.

title: Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison
text:
The Method
The fitContinuous() function in the geiger package fits all eight models to a named trait vector and a phylogeny. Each model transforms the tree’s branch lengths or variance-covariance structure in a different way to best fit the observed trait data.
Here is what each model captures:

BM (Brownian motion): Random drift at a constant rate. The null model.
OU (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck): Drift with a “rubber band” pulling toward an optimum. Stabilizing selection.
EB (Early Burst): Rate of evolution decays exponentially from root to tips. Adaptive radiation signature.
Lambda: Scales the internal branch lengths (0 = star tree, 1 = original tree). Tests phylogenetic signal strength directly.
Kappa: Raises branch lengths to a power. Kappa < 1 = punctuational (change concentrated at nodes). Kappa > 1 = gradual (change proportional to time).
Delta: Raises path lengths to a power. Delta < 1 = early change. Delta > 1 = late change.
Trend: Brownian motion with a directional drift — the trait mean shifts systematically over time.
White noise: No phylogenetic structure at all. Every species is drawn independently from a single distribution.

We compare all eight using AICc (corrected Akaike Information Criterion, which penalizes extra parameters more strongly with small sample sizes). The model with the lowest AICc is preferred, and Akaike weights quantify the relative support for each model.

title: Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison
text:
How to Interpret Results








Winning model
Biological interpretation
What to say on your poster




BM
Neutral drift at constant rate
“Color evolves as a random walk with no detectable directional or selective pressure.”


OU
Stabilizing selection toward an optimum
“Color is constrained by stabilizing selection — lineages that stray too far are pulled back toward a family-level optimum.”


EB
Early burst, rates slow down
“Color diversified rapidly early in the family’s history and has since slowed, consistent with early niche filling.”


Lambda (low)
Weak phylogenetic signal
“Phylogeny is a poor predictor of color — closely related species are no more similar than expected by chance.”


Kappa (< 1)
Punctuational evolution
“Color changes are concentrated at speciation events rather than accumulating gradually along branches.”


Delta (< 1)
Early change dominates
“Most color evolution occurred early in the family’s history, with little change in recent branches.”


Delta (> 1)
Late change dominates
“Color evolution has accelerated toward the present, with most change in recent lineages.”


Trend
Directional evolution
“Color has evolved directionally over time — there is a systematic trend toward [higher/lower] values.”


White noise
No phylogenetic structure
“Color variation shows no phylogenetic structure at all — the tree contains no information about color similarity.”









Common pitfalls




Overfitting with 8 models and small trees: With < 40 species, AICc differences among models may be too small to be meaningful. Focus on the top 2–3 models and whether they tell a consistent story.
Lambda and OU can mimic each other. Both capture “less phylogenetic signal than expected.” If both rank near the top, the key result is that signal is reduced — the specific mechanism (branch scaling vs. rubber band) may be indistinguishable.
Trend requires a root-to-tip direction. The trend model assumes time flows from root to tips. It is only meaningful for ultrametric (time-calibrated) trees.
Do not interpret winning model parameters in isolation. A kappa of 0.8 that wins by 1 AICc unit over BM is a weak result. Always report the deltaAICc and Akaike weights alongside the winning model.
This extends Recipe 20. If you have already run Recipe 20, you can report the extended comparison as a sensitivity analysis that confirms or refines your earlier result.

title: Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison ─────────────
# Requires the geiger package.
# If not installed: install.packages("geiger")

source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, ggplot2, theme_poster
library(geiger)

# ── 1. Load your tree and pavo data ───────────────────────────────
bundle   <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")
pavo_csv <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# ── 2. Match tree to data ─────────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, pavo_csv, species_col = "species")
tree    <- matched$tree
dat     <- matched$data

cat("Working with", length(tree$tip.label), "species\n")

# ── 3. Check ultrametric ──────────────────────────────────────────
if (!ape::is.ultrametric(tree)) {
  cat("Forcing ultrametric tree (small numerical correction)\n")
  tree <- phytools::force.ultrametric(tree, method = "extend")
}

# ── 4. Build PC1 as focal trait ───────────────────────────────────
pavo_vars <- c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL")

complete <- complete.cases(dat[, pavo_vars])
if (any(!complete)) {
  cat("Dropping", sum(!complete), "species with missing values\n")
}
dat_complete <- dat[complete, ]
tree         <- ape::drop.tip(tree,
                              setdiff(tree$tip.label, dat_complete$species))

trait_mat           <- dat_complete[, pavo_vars]
rownames(trait_mat) <- dat_complete$species
trait_mat           <- trait_mat[tree$tip.label, ]

pca <- prcomp(trait_mat, scale. = TRUE)
pc1 <- setNames(pca$x[, 1], rownames(pca$x))

var_explained <- round(summary(pca)$importance[2, 1] * 100, 1)
cat("PC1 explains", var_explained, "% of color pattern variance\n")

# ── 5. Fit all 8 evolutionary models ─────────────────────────────
models <- c("BM", "OU", "EB", "lambda", "kappa", "delta", "trend", "white")

fits <- lapply(setNames(models, models), function(m) {
  tryCatch(
    fitContinuous(tree, pc1, model = m),
    error = function(e) {
      message("Model '", m, "' failed: ", e$message)
      NULL
    }
  )
})

# Remove any models that failed
fits <- fits[!sapply(fits, is.null)]
cat("Successfully fit", length(fits), "of", length(models), "models\n")

# ── 6. Build AICc comparison table ───────────────────────────────
aic_table <- data.frame(
  Model    = names(fits),
  AICc     = sapply(fits, function(f) f$opt$aicc),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
aic_table$deltaAICc <- round(aic_table$AICc - min(aic_table$AICc), 2)
aic_table$weight    <- round(
  exp(-0.5 * aic_table$deltaAICc) /
  sum(exp(-0.5 * aic_table$deltaAICc)), 3
)
aic_table$AICc      <- round(aic_table$AICc, 2)
aic_table           <- aic_table[order(aic_table$deltaAICc), ]

cat("\n── Extended Model Comparison (PC1) ─────────────────────────\n")
print(aic_table, row.names = FALSE)

best <- aic_table$Model[1]
cat("\nBest model:", best, "(Akaike weight =", aic_table$weight[1], ")\n")

# ── 7. Report key parameters for the best model ──────────────────
cat("\n── Best model parameters ──────────────────────────────────\n")
best_fit <- fits[[best]]
if (best == "lambda") {
  cat("  lambda:", round(best_fit$opt$lambda, 3), "\n")
  if (best_fit$opt$lambda < 0.3) cat("  → Weak phylogenetic signal\n")
} else if (best == "kappa") {
  cat("  kappa:", round(best_fit$opt$kappa, 3), "\n")
  if (best_fit$opt$kappa < 1) cat("  → Punctuational evolution\n")
  if (best_fit$opt$kappa > 1) cat("  → Gradual evolution\n")
} else if (best == "delta") {
  cat("  delta:", round(best_fit$opt$delta, 3), "\n")
  if (best_fit$opt$delta < 1) cat("  → Early change dominates\n")
  if (best_fit$opt$delta > 1) cat("  → Late change dominates\n")
} else if (best == "trend") {
  cat("  slope:", round(best_fit$opt$slope, 4), "\n")
  cat("  → Directional trend in color over time\n")
} else if (best == "OU") {
  cat("  alpha:", round(best_fit$opt$alpha, 4), "\n")
  if (best_fit$opt$alpha < 0.01) cat("  → alpha near zero: OU ≈ BM\n")
} else if (best == "EB") {
  cat("  a (rate decay):", round(best_fit$opt$a, 4), "\n")
  if (abs(best_fit$opt$a) < 0.001) cat("  → a near zero: EB ≈ BM\n")
}

# ── 8. Bar chart of Akaike weights ───────────────────────────────
aic_table$Model <- factor(aic_table$Model, levels = aic_table$Model)

ggplot(aic_table, aes(x = Model, y = weight, fill = Model)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, width = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Akaike weights across 8 evolutionary models (PC1)",
       x = "", y = "Akaike weight") +
  theme_poster +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))

ggsave("results/recipe22-model-weights-pc1.pdf", width = 9, height = 6)
cat("Saved: results/recipe22-model-weights-pc1.pdf\n")

# ── 9. Heatmap: all traits x all models ──────────────────────────
# Run model comparison for each pavo variable + PC1
all_traits <- c(pavo_vars, "PC1")
heatmap_data <- data.frame()

for (v in all_traits) {
  if (v == "PC1") {
    x <- pc1
  } else {
    x <- setNames(dat_complete[[v]], dat_complete$species)
    x <- x[tree$tip.label]
  }

  for (m in models) {
    fit <- tryCatch(
      fitContinuous(tree, x, model = m),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
    if (!is.null(fit)) {
      heatmap_data <- rbind(heatmap_data, data.frame(
        trait = v, model = m, aicc = fit$opt$aicc,
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      ))
    }
  }
}

# Compute weights within each trait
library(dplyr)
heatmap_data <- heatmap_data %>%
  group_by(trait) %>%
  mutate(
    delta_aicc = aicc - min(aicc),
    weight = exp(-0.5 * delta_aicc) / sum(exp(-0.5 * delta_aicc))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Plot heatmap
heatmap_data$trait <- factor(heatmap_data$trait, levels = rev(all_traits))
heatmap_data$model <- factor(heatmap_data$model, levels = models)

ggplot(heatmap_data, aes(x = model, y = trait, fill = weight)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(weight, 2)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#2a9d8f",
                      name = "Akaike\nweight") +
  labs(title = "Model support across color variables",
       x = "Evolutionary model", y = "Color variable") +
  theme_poster +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))

ggsave("results/recipe22-model-heatmap.pdf", width = 10, height = 7)
cat("Saved: results/recipe22-model-heatmap.pdf\n")

title: Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison
text:
From the Literature

Pagel, M. (1999) — Introduced the lambda, kappa, and delta branch-length transformations for testing the tempo and mode of trait evolution on phylogenies. Lambda tests phylogenetic signal, kappa tests punctuational vs. gradual change, and delta tests early vs. late change. These three transformations remain the standard tools for exploring how trait evolution departs from Brownian motion. Nature, 401(6756), 877–884. DOI


Harmon, L. J., Losos, J. B., Davies, T. J., Gillespie, R. G., Gittleman, J. L., Jennings, W. B., … & Mooers, A. O. (2010) — Systematically evaluated BM, OU, and EB models across hundreds of comparative datasets using fitContinuous(), finding that early burst is surprisingly rare. This paper provides the analytical framework and the geiger implementation used in this recipe. Evolution, 64(8), 2385–2396. DOI

title: Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time
text: Did the major axes of color pattern variation in my family originate early in its history and then slow down, or have color patterns continued to diversify at a steady pace all the way to the present?

title: Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time
text: Did the major axes of color pattern variation in my family originate early in its history and then slow down, or have color patterns continued to diversify at a steady pace all the way to the present?

title: Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Macroevolutionary tempo analysis



Disparity-through-time (DTT) analysis asks how morphological (or color) diversity was distributed across the tree at each moment in evolutionary history. It works by computing, for each internal node, the average pairwise disparity within subclades descending from that node, then watching how that subclade disparity changes as you move from the root toward the tips. If subclades partition color space early — each major lineage staking out its own region — disparity within subclades will be low relative to total disparity, and you get a negative MDI. If subclades overlap in color space and diversification is ongoing, disparity within subclades stays high relative to total disparity, and you get a positive MDI. This is one of the few macroevolutionary methods that directly tests whether an adaptive radiation “front-loaded” its diversity.

title: Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Reef fish families differ enormously in whether their color diversity looks early-burst or gradual. Some families, like angelfishes, have iconic deep-clade differences in color pattern (adults vs. juveniles, planktivores vs. cleaners) that were established millions of years ago. Others, like wrasses, show more recent explosions of color in sexual signals. DTT analysis gives you a visual and quantitative answer to which pattern dominates in your family. It also connects directly to lectures on macroevolutionary rates (Lec 18) — you are putting your family’s color evolution on the same framework used to study entire adaptive radiations.






Clade-specific tips




Pomacanthidae (angelfishes): The juvenile–adult color difference is a developmental, not evolutionary, pattern — make sure your pavo metrics all come from adult photographs. If early diverging genera (e.g., Pomacanthus) have very different color from derived genera (e.g., Centropyge), expect a negative MDI: early lineages staked out very different color space.
Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): The extreme color diversity in this tribe is largely concentrated in Cirrhilabrus and Paracheilinus. Whether this shows as early or late on the DTT curve depends on where the tribe-level split falls relative to the species-level diversification within these genera.
Hypsigenyinae (hogfishes and allies): With only ~38 species, your DTT null envelope will be wide. A non-significant MDI does not mean the pattern is absent — report MDI and interpret it qualitatively even if the p-value is borderline.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): The two families (Balistidae and Monacanthidae) diverged early and have quite different color strategies. If your bundle spans both, expect early-burst signal from that deep split.

title: Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time
text:
The Method
DTT uses your pavo trait matrix and your time-calibrated phylogeny to compute subclade disparity at each internal node. The dtt() function in the geiger package does the heavy lifting. It then compares the observed DTT curve against a Brownian motion null, generated by simulating 1,000 random datasets on the same tree. The morphological disparity index (MDI) is the signed area between the observed DTT curve and the Brownian motion median. Positive MDI means your observed disparity stays higher than expected under drift (subclades overlap — late-filling color space); negative MDI means your observed disparity falls below expected (subclades are partitioned — early-burst pattern).
The input should be a matrix where rows are species and columns are your pavo variables (m, A, Jc, Jt, m_dS, m_dL). Using all six variables jointly captures overall color pattern disparity rather than any single axis.
This analysis requires the geiger package. If it is not installed, run install.packages("geiger") once before sourcing helpers.

title: Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time
text:
How to Interpret Results








MDI
Meaning
What to say on your poster




MDI > 0 (p < 0.05)
Subclades overlap in color space — ongoing diversification, clades have not partitioned color axes
“Color pattern diversity accumulated gradually and continuously; major clades have not converged on distinct color strategies.”


MDI < 0 (p < 0.05)
Subclades partitioned — early niche partitioning, each major clade occupies distinct color space
“Color pattern diversity shows an early-burst signature: major color axes were established early in the family’s history and subsequent diversification filled within-clade space.”


MDI ~ 0 (p > 0.05)
Observed trajectory matches Brownian motion expectation
“Color pattern disparity accumulates at a rate consistent with neutral evolutionary drift, without strong evidence for either early burst or recent acceleration.”


p-value marginally significant (0.05–0.10)
Borderline
Report MDI and direction; note that your sample size may limit power.









Common pitfalls




DTT requires a time-calibrated (ultrametric) tree. Check that your tree is ultrametric before running: ape::is.ultrametric(tree). If it returns FALSE, small numerical errors from tree-building may be to blame; try phytools::force.ultrametric(tree) to correct them, and report that you did so.
Interpret the MDI in light of your tree shape. A heavily pectinate (ladder-shaped) tree will produce different null expectations than a balanced tree. The Brownian motion simulation envelope accounts for this, but if your tree is very asymmetric, the envelope will be wide and power will be lower.
Missing data affects disparity estimates. If some species lack values for one or more pavo variables, remove them before building the trait matrix. Do not impute missing values for this analysis.
DTT is a whole-tree summary. It does not tell you which node drove the early burst. If you want to identify the responsible clade, compare DTT curves for subclades separately (run dtt() on pruned subtrees).

title: Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time ───────────────────────────
# Requires the geiger package.
# If not installed: install.packages("geiger")

source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, ggplot2, theme_poster
library(geiger)

# ── 1. Load your tree and pavo data ─────────────────────────────
bundle   <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")
pavo_csv <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# ── 2. Match tree to data ───────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, pavo_csv, species_col = "species")
tree    <- matched$tree
dat     <- matched$data

cat("Working with", length(tree$tip.label), "species\n")

# ── 3. Check that tree is ultrametric ───────────────────────────
if (!ape::is.ultrametric(tree)) {
  cat("Tree is not ultrametric — forcing ultrametric (small numerical fix)\n")
  tree <- phytools::force.ultrametric(tree, method = "extend")
}

# ── 4. Build trait matrix ───────────────────────────────────────
pavo_vars <- c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL")
complete  <- complete.cases(dat[, pavo_vars])
if (any(!complete)) {
  cat("Dropping", sum(!complete), "species with missing pavo values\n")
}
dat_complete <- dat[complete, ]
tree         <- ape::drop.tip(tree,
                              setdiff(tree$tip.label, dat_complete$species))

trait_mat            <- as.matrix(dat_complete[, pavo_vars])
rownames(trait_mat)  <- dat_complete$species
trait_mat            <- trait_mat[tree$tip.label, ]   # align row order

cat("Final sample for DTT:", nrow(trait_mat), "species\n")

# ── 5. DTT analysis with 1000 simulations ───────────────────────
set.seed(42)   # for reproducibility
dtt_result <- dtt(tree, trait_mat, nsim = 1000, plot = FALSE)

# ── 6. Compute p-value and report MDI ─────────────────────────────
# geiger's dtt() returns MDI but not always a p-value (depends on
# package version). We compute it from the simulation matrix:
# for each BM simulation, compute its MDI, then ask what fraction
# of simulated MDIs are >= the observed MDI.
bm_median <- apply(dtt_result$sim, 1, median, na.rm = TRUE)
sim_mdis  <- apply(dtt_result$sim, 2, function(s) mean(s - bm_median))
obs_mdi   <- as.numeric(dtt_result$MDI)
mdi_pval  <- mean(sim_mdis >= obs_mdi)

cat("\n── Disparity-Through-Time results ──\n")
cat("MDI (morphological disparity index):", round(obs_mdi, 3), "\n")
cat("p-value (proportion of BM sims with MDI >= observed):",
    round(mdi_pval, 3), "\n")

if (obs_mdi > 0) {
  cat("Interpretation: subclades OVERLAP in color space (MDI > 0)\n")
  cat("  Color diversity has accumulated continuously; no early partitioning.\n")
} else {
  cat("Interpretation: subclades are PARTITIONED in color space (MDI < 0)\n")
  cat("  Early-burst signature: major color axes established early.\n")
}

# ── 7. Helper function to plot a DTT result ───────────────────────
# geiger 2.0.11 does not provide a plot method for dtt objects,
# so we draw the DTT envelope manually.
plot_dtt <- function(dtt_obj, main = "Disparity Through Time", ...) {
  times     <- dtt_obj$times
  obs_curve <- dtt_obj$dtt
  sim_lower <- apply(dtt_obj$sim, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)
  sim_upper <- apply(dtt_obj$sim, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)
  sim_med   <- apply(dtt_obj$sim, 1, median, na.rm = TRUE)

  plot(times, obs_curve, type = "n",
       ylim = range(c(obs_curve, sim_lower, sim_upper), na.rm = TRUE),
       main = main,
       xlab = "Relative time (root = 0, tips = 1)",
       ylab = "Average subclade disparity", ...)
  polygon(c(times, rev(times)), c(sim_lower, rev(sim_upper)),
          col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.1), border = NA)
  lines(times, sim_med, col = "grey50", lty = 2)
  lines(times, obs_curve, col = "black", lwd = 2)
}

# ── 7b. Save DTT plot as PDF ─────────────────────────────────────
pdf("results/recipe19-dtt.pdf", width = 8, height = 6)
plot_dtt(dtt_result,
         main = "Disparity Through Time — Color Pattern")
mtext(paste0("MDI = ", round(obs_mdi, 3),
             "  (p = ", round(mdi_pval, 3), ")"),
      side = 1, line = -2, adj = 0.05, cex = 0.9)
dev.off()
cat("Saved: results/recipe19-dtt.pdf\n")

# ── 8. Optional: DTT for individual pavo variables ──────────────
# Run DTT separately for each variable to see which drives the pattern.
pdf("results/recipe19-dtt-by-variable.pdf", width = 12, height = 8)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (v in pavo_vars) {
  x_vec            <- setNames(dat_complete[[v]], dat_complete$species)
  x_vec            <- x_vec[tree$tip.label]
  x_mat            <- matrix(x_vec, ncol = 1,
                             dimnames = list(names(x_vec), v))
  dtt_v <- tryCatch(
    dtt(tree, x_mat, nsim = 200, plot = FALSE),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (!is.null(dtt_v)) {
    bm_med_v   <- apply(dtt_v$sim, 1, median, na.rm = TRUE)
    sim_mdis_v <- apply(dtt_v$sim, 2, function(s) mean(s - bm_med_v))
    mdi_v      <- as.numeric(dtt_v$MDI)
    pval_v     <- mean(sim_mdis_v >= mdi_v)

    plot_dtt(dtt_v, main = v)
    mtext(paste0("MDI=", round(mdi_v, 2), " p=", round(pval_v, 2)),
          side = 1, line = -1.5, adj = 0.05, cex = 0.75)
  }
}
dev.off()
cat("Saved: results/recipe19-dtt-by-variable.pdf\n")

title: Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time
text:
From the Literature

Harmon, L. J., Schulte, J. A., II, Larson, A., & Losos, J. B. (2003) — Introduced the disparity-through-time framework and the MDI statistic by applying it to iguanian lizard radiations. Showed that Anolis lizards show a classic adaptive radiation pattern (early partitioning of ecomorphs) while other iguanians do not. This paper is the primary reference for the DTT method. Science, 301(5635), 961–964. DOI


Slater, G. J., Price, S. A., Santini, F., & Alfaro, M. E. (2010) — Applied DTT analysis to body size evolution in elopomorph fishes, showing that this diverse lineage does not show an early-burst pattern despite being an ancient radiation. A good example of how to report and interpret a non-significant or positive MDI result. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 277(1687), 1563–1569. DOI


Melville, J., Harmon, L. J., & Losos, J. B. (2006) — Used DTT to compare color and morphological disparity in Ctenotus skinks, demonstrating that color and body shape can show different macroevolutionary tempos within the same clade — a useful precedent for interpreting divergent results across your six pavo variables. Evolution, 60(8), 1577–1587. DOI

title: Recipe 18: Biogeographic Color Variation
text: Do species from the Atlantic show different color pattern diversity than Indo-Pacific species in the same family, or does the ocean basin a lineage lives in have no detectable influence on color evolution?

title: Recipe 18: Biogeographic Color Variation
text: Do species from the Atlantic show different color pattern diversity than Indo-Pacific species in the same family, or does the ocean basin a lineage lives in have no detectable influence on color evolution?

title: Recipe 18: Biogeographic Color Variation
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Biogeographic comparison / natural experiment



Ocean basins are among the most powerful natural experiments in evolutionary biology. The closure of the Isthmus of Panama ~3 million years ago separated Atlantic and Pacific populations of the same ancestral lineages, and the deep break between the Atlantic and Indo-Pacific goes back much further. By treating basin as a categorical predictor in a phylogenetic model, you are asking whether the evolutionary and ecological context of each basin — different species richness, different competitors, different light environments — has pushed color patterns in detectably different directions. This is the comparative method applied to geography rather than ecology.

title: Recipe 18: Biogeographic Color Variation
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
The Atlantic and Indo-Pacific differ dramatically in reef fish diversity, habitat complexity, and the ecological roles color plays. The Indo-Pacific hosts far more reef fish species, potentially driving greater diversification of color signals for species recognition. The Atlantic, with fewer species, may rely less on fine-grained color discrimination. Testing this hypothesis with pavo metrics turns a qualitative observation into a quantifiable claim.






Clade-specific tips




Halichoerine wrasses (tribe Julidini and relatives): Several genera contain geminate species pairs — Atlantic sister species separated from Pacific relatives by the Isthmus of Panama. These pairs are a particularly clean biogeographic signal because the divergence time is known (~3 Mya). If your bundle contains Halichoeres or Thalassoma species from both basins, you have a textbook natural experiment.
Scarinae (parrotfishes): Sparisoma is almost entirely Atlantic; Scarus is almost entirely Indo-Pacific. This means your basin comparison is partly confounded with genus-level differences. Phrase your interpretation carefully: you are comparing Atlantic Sparisoma-grade color to Indo-Pacific Scarus-grade color, not controlling for that evolutionary split.
Pomacanthidae (angelfishes): Several genera (e.g., Centropyge, Holacanthus) have Atlantic and Indo-Pacific representatives. Make sure your basin coding reflects the actual range of each species, not just the genus home range.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): Several triggerfish genera span both basins. Check FishBase range maps for each species individually; do not assume genus-level distribution.

title: Recipe 18: Biogeographic Color Variation
text:
The Method
You have two ways to assign species to basins. Option A (recommended) is to code basin by hand from range maps. Open FishBase or your reference literature, look at each species’ known range, and write a two-column CSV with species and basin (values: Atlantic, Indo-Pacific, or both). This takes 30–60 minutes but gives you accurate, defensible assignments. Species coded both — those that genuinely span both basins — should be excluded, because they do not test the question.
Option B uses FishBase’s stocks() function to pull geographic bounding boxes for each species and classifies them by longitude. This is faster but less reliable: FishBase bounding boxes can be imprecise, and some widespread species get misclassified. If you use Option B, spot-check at least a quarter of your assignments against known range maps.
Once basins are assigned, you run a PGLS with basin as a categorical predictor and your color metric of interest (typically Jc, color diversity) as the response. PGLS controls for the non-independence introduced by shared ancestry, so your basin comparison is not inflated by the fact that Atlantic species share an evolutionary history with each other independent of basin effects.

title: Recipe 18: Biogeographic Color Variation
text:
How to Interpret Results








Result
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Significant basin effect (p < 0.05), Atlantic > Indo-Pacific
Atlantic species show higher color diversity per species, possibly because fewer species must be distinguished via color
“Color pattern diversity is unexpectedly higher in the Atlantic despite lower overall species richness.”


Significant basin effect (p < 0.05), Indo-Pacific > Atlantic
Greater color diversity in the species-rich Indo-Pacific, consistent with species recognition pressure
“Color pattern diversity tracks regional species richness, with Indo-Pacific species showing significantly more complex color patterns.”


Non-significant basin effect (p > 0.05)
Basin does not predict color pattern diversity once phylogeny is accounted for
“Ocean basin does not significantly predict color diversity, suggesting color evolution in this family is driven by factors other than regional species richness.”


Small or unequal sample sizes
Results unreliable regardless of p-value
Report both group sizes and interpret cautiously.









Common pitfalls




Unequal sample sizes per basin will affect power. If you have 40 Indo-Pacific species and 8 Atlantic species, a non-significant result may simply reflect low power in the smaller group. Always report n per basin in your poster.
Do not exclude both species silently. Report how many species you dropped as both and why. If more than 20% of your sample is excluded, the remaining comparison may be non-representative.
Basin is partly confounded with phylogeny. Atlantic and Indo-Pacific lineages often diverged deep in the tree, meaning basin and clade are correlated. PGLS mitigates but does not fully eliminate this — be honest about this limitation.
FishBase bounding boxes (Option B) can misclassify species. If you use the automated approach, validate a random subset and report how many species you hand-checked.

title: Recipe 18: Biogeographic Color Variation
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 18: Biogeographic Color Variation ────────────────────
source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, ggplot2, theme_poster

# ── 1. Load your tree and pavo data ─────────────────────────────
bundle   <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")
pavo_csv <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# ── 2A. Option A (recommended): hand-coded basin assignments ────
# Create a CSV with two columns: species, basin
# basin values: "Atlantic", "Indo-Pacific", or "both"
# Example row: Halichoeres_bivittatus, Atlantic
basins <- read.csv("my_basin_codes.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Merge with pavo metrics
merged <- merge(pavo_csv, basins, by = "species")

# Exclude species that span both basins
n_both <- sum(merged$basin == "both")
cat("Excluding", n_both, "species coded as 'both'\n")
merged <- merged[merged$basin != "both", ]

# Report sample sizes per basin
cat("Atlantic species:", sum(merged$basin == "Atlantic"), "\n")
cat("Indo-Pacific species:", sum(merged$basin == "Indo-Pacific"), "\n")

# ── 2B. Option B (automated, less reliable): FishBase ranges ────
# Uncomment this block if you prefer automated assignment.
# library(rfishbase)
# stocks_data <- rfishbase::stocks(pavo_csv$species)
# stocks_data <- stocks_data[!duplicated(stocks_data$Species), ]
# stocks_data$basin <- ifelse(
#   stocks_data$EasternLongitude < -20 & stocks_data$WesternLongitude > -100,
#   "Atlantic",
#   ifelse(stocks_data$WesternLongitude >= 20, "Indo-Pacific", "both")
# )
# merged <- merge(pavo_csv,
#                 stocks_data[, c("Species", "basin")],
#                 by.x = "species", by.y = "Species")
# merged <- merged[merged$basin != "both", ]

# ── 3. Match tree to merged data ────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, merged, species_col = "species")
tree    <- matched$tree
dat     <- matched$data

cat("Final sample:", length(tree$tip.label), "species\n")

# ── 4. PGLS: Jc ~ basin ─────────────────────────────────────────
model <- safe_pgls(Jc ~ basin, df = dat, tree = tree)
summary(model)

# Extract key numbers for the poster
coefs <- summary(model)$tTable
cat("\n── PGLS result ──\n")
cat("basin effect estimate:", round(coefs["basinIndo-Pacific", "Value"], 3), "\n")
cat("p-value:", round(coefs["basinIndo-Pacific", "p-value"], 4), "\n")

# ── 5. Boxplot with jittered points ─────────────────────────────
ggplot(dat, aes(x = basin, y = Jc, fill = basin)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 3, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    title = "Color diversity by ocean basin",
    x     = "",
    y     = "Color diversity (Jc)"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Atlantic" = "#0077b6", "Indo-Pacific" = "#e76f51")
  ) +
  theme_poster +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

ggsave("results/recipe18-basin-boxplot.pdf", width = 7, height = 6)
cat("Saved: results/recipe18-basin-boxplot.pdf\n")

# ── 6. Optional: run for all 6 pavo variables ───────────────────
pavo_vars <- c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL")
basin_results <- data.frame(
  Variable = character(0),
  estimate = numeric(0),
  p_value  = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (v in pavo_vars) {
  formula_str <- paste(v, "~ basin")
  mod <- tryCatch(
    safe_pgls(as.formula(formula_str), df = dat, tree = tree),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (!is.null(mod)) {
    tt <- summary(mod)$tTable
    row_name <- grep("basin", rownames(tt), value = TRUE)[1]
    basin_results <- rbind(basin_results, data.frame(
      Variable = v,
      estimate = round(tt[row_name, "Value"], 3),
      p_value  = round(tt[row_name, "p-value"], 4),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
  }
}
cat("\n── Basin effects across all pavo variables ──\n")
print(basin_results)

title: Recipe 5: Measurement Robustness
text: If I had used a different photograph of each species, would my phylogenetic signal results change — or are my conclusions robust to the inevitable noise in single-image measurements?

title: Recipe 5: Measurement Robustness
text: If I had used a different photograph of each species, would my phylogenetic signal results change — or are my conclusions robust to the inevitable noise in single-image measurements?

title: Recipe 5: Measurement Robustness
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Sensitivity analysis / uncertainty quantification



Every measurement has error. In our pipeline, a single photograph represents an entire species, but different photographs of the same species can produce different pavo statistics (different lighting, angle, background, color calibration, individual variation). Sensitivity analysis asks: how much do my conclusions depend on this measurement noise? Monte Carlo resampling quantifies this by repeating the analysis hundreds of times, each time adding realistic noise to every tip value, and checking whether the key results (K values, PCA loadings, PGLS slopes) remain stable. If they do, the conclusions are robust. If they scatter widely, the signal may not survive honest uncertainty.

title: Recipe 5: Measurement Robustness
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Your pavo metrics come from one exemplar image per species. That image was chosen as representative, but it is still a sample of one. In Demo 8, you measured five different images of a single “error species” and quantified how much each pavo variable fluctuates across photographs. That within-species standard deviation is your estimate of measurement error. This recipe injects that noise into every species in your dataset and asks whether your Recipe 1 K values, your Recipe 3 PCA loadings, and your PGLS slopes survive the perturbation.






Clade-specific tips




Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): Male fairy wrasses can display dramatically different colors depending on behavioral context (nuptial flash vs. resting). If your error species happens to include both display and resting photos, your error SD may be large. That is a real source of biological noise, not a measurement artifact — flag it on your poster.
Scarinae (parrotfishes): Initial-phase and terminal-phase parrotfish look like different species. If any of your five error-species images includes a different phase, exclude it before estimating the SD.
Acanthuridae (surgeonfishes): Surgeonfishes are relatively consistent in coloration across photographs, so expect small error SDs. Your MC distributions should be tight.

title: Recipe 5: Measurement Robustness
text:
The Method
The Monte Carlo approach is straightforward. You have a trait matrix (species x 6 pavo variables) and a per-variable standard deviation estimated from the five-image error species in Demo 8. On each of 200 iterations, the algorithm adds independent Gaussian noise to every cell of the trait matrix (with SD equal to the per-variable error SD), then re-runs the same analyses: Blomberg’s K for each variable, PCA loadings, and PGLS slopes. After 200 iterations, you have a distribution of each statistic rather than a single point estimate.
The key diagnostic is the K boxplot: for each pavo variable, plot the distribution of K values across 200 MC iterations alongside the observed K (marked as a diamond). If the observed K sits clearly above the MC distribution, the signal is robust — it exceeds what measurement noise alone could produce. If the observed K falls within the MC distribution, measurement noise could account for the entire signal, and you cannot confidently claim that phylogenetic structure is real.
The same logic applies to PCA loadings and PGLS slopes. If the loading of m on PC1 is +0.55 in your real data but ranges from -0.2 to +0.7 across MC iterations, the axis interpretation is fragile. If it stays between +0.45 and +0.65, the axis is stable.

title: Recipe 5: Measurement Robustness
text:
How to Interpret Results








Observation
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Observed K is above the 97.5th percentile of the MC distribution
K is robust: measurement noise cannot explain the signal
“Phylogenetic signal survives measurement noise (observed K above 97.5% of Monte Carlo distribution).”


Observed K falls within the MC interquartile range
K is fragile: noise could produce an equally large K
“The observed phylogenetic signal does not clearly exceed measurement noise, so this result should be interpreted cautiously.”


MC distribution is very narrow (small boxes on boxplot)
Error SDs are small — your measurements are precise
“Pavo statistics are highly repeatable across photographs; MC distributions are narrow.”


MC distribution is very wide
Error SDs are large — results are sensitive to image choice
“Substantial measurement noise; results should be validated with additional images per species.”


Some variables robust, others fragile
Different aspects of the pattern have different signal-to-noise ratios
“Signal in [variable] is robust, but signal in [variable] is within measurement noise, suggesting that [robust variable] carries the reliable phylogenetic information.”









Common pitfalls




If your observed K falls within the MC distribution, the signal may not survive measurement noise. This does not mean there is no signal — it means you cannot distinguish real signal from noise with your current data. More images per species (reducing the error SD) would tighten the MC distribution.
The error SD from one species is applied to all species. This assumes measurement noise is roughly constant across the family. If your error species is unusually variable (e.g., a sexually dichromatic species photographed in both morphs), your SD overestimates the noise for most other species and the MC test becomes overly conservative.
200 iterations is a minimum. For a poster, 200 is enough to see the shape of the distribution. For a publication, 1,000+ iterations would be standard. Do not increase beyond 200 in class unless you have time to wait.

title: Recipe 5: Measurement Robustness
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 5: Measurement Robustness ──────────────────────────
source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, ggplot2, theme_poster

# ── 1. Load the MC helper from Demo 8 ─────────────────────────
# This script defines mc_redo_analyses(), which runs the full
# Monte Carlo perturbation loop.
source("path/to/demo8-folder/scripts/error-aware-analyses.R")

# ── 2. Load your bundle and pavo data ──────────────────────────
bundle   <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")
pavo_csv <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# ── 3. Match tree to data ──────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, pavo_csv, species_col = "species")
tree    <- matched$tree
dat     <- matched$data

# ── 4. Build trait matrix ──────────────────────────────────────
pavo_vars <- c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL")
trait_mat <- as.matrix(dat[, pavo_vars])
rownames(trait_mat) <- dat$species

# Drop rows with NA and prune tree to match
complete  <- complete.cases(trait_mat)
trait_mat <- trait_mat[complete, ]
tree_mc   <- ape::drop.tip(tree,
                            setdiff(tree$tip.label, rownames(trait_mat)))
trait_mat <- trait_mat[tree_mc$tip.label, ]

# ── 5. Define error SDs from your 5-image error species ───────
# Replace these values with the SDs you computed in Demo 8 Part 3.
# Each number is the standard deviation of that pavo variable
# across the 5 images of your error species.
error_sd <- c(
  m    = 0.02,    # <-- your SD for transition density
  A    = 0.05,    # <-- your SD for aspect ratio
  Jc   = 0.03,    # <-- your SD for chromatic diversity
  Jt   = 0.02,    # <-- your SD for transition diversity
  m_dS = 0.01,    # <-- your SD for chromatic boundary strength
  m_dL = 0.01     # <-- your SD for achromatic boundary strength
)
# IMPORTANT: replace the placeholder values above with your
# actual error SDs from Demo 8's 5-image measurement.

# ── 6. Run Monte Carlo (200 iterations) ───────────────────────
cat("Running 200 MC iterations (this takes a few minutes)...\n")
mc <- mc_redo_analyses(trait_mat, tree_mc, error_sd,
                       n_iter = 200, seed = 2026)

# ── 7. Compute observed K values for comparison ───────────────
obs_K <- sapply(pavo_vars, function(v) {
  x <- setNames(trait_mat[, v], rownames(trait_mat))
  phytools::phylosig(tree_mc, x, method = "K")
})

# ── 8. K boxplot: observed vs. MC distribution ────────────────
# Reshape MC K values for plotting
K_long <- data.frame(
  variable = rep(colnames(mc$K), each = nrow(mc$K)),
  K_mc     = as.vector(mc$K),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Observed K as a separate data frame for the diamond overlay
obs_df <- data.frame(
  variable = names(obs_K),
  K_obs    = as.numeric(obs_K),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

p <- ggplot(K_long, aes(x = variable, y = K_mc)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey85", color = "grey50", outlier.size = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = obs_df,
             aes(x = variable, y = K_obs),
             shape = 18, size = 5, color = "#c14a4a") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey40") +
  labs(
    title    = "Measurement robustness: observed K vs. MC noise distribution",
    subtitle = "Red diamond = observed K; boxes = 200 MC iterations with measurement noise",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Blomberg's K"
  ) +
  theme_poster

print(p)

# ── 9. Save poster-quality PDF ─────────────────────────────────
ggsave("results/recipe5-mc-robustness.pdf", p, width = 12, height = 8)
cat("Saved: results/recipe5-mc-robustness.pdf\n")

# ── 10. Print summary: which variables are robust? ─────────────
cat("\n── Robustness summary ──\n")
for (v in pavo_vars) {
  mc_vals  <- mc$K[, v]
  mc_upper <- quantile(mc_vals, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)
  mc_lower <- quantile(mc_vals, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)
  obs      <- obs_K[v]
  robust   <- obs > mc_upper
  cat(sprintf("  %-5s  obs K = %.3f   MC 95%% CI = [%.3f, %.3f]   %s\n",
              v, obs, mc_lower, mc_upper,
              if (robust) "ROBUST" else "within noise"))
}

title: Recipe 5: Measurement Robustness
text:
From the Literature

Blomberg, S. P., Garland, T., Jr., & Ives, A. R. (2003) — The K statistic tested in this recipe’s MC loop; established the permutation framework for significance testing, which the MC approach extends to measurement uncertainty. Evolution, 57(4), 717–745. DOI


Alfaro, M. E., Karan, E. A., Schwartz, S. T., & Shultz, A. J. (2019) — Discussed measurement considerations for pavo adjacency statistics in the context of single-image-per-species datasets, noting that classification noise (k-means variability) adds to photographic noise. Integrative and Comparative Biology, 59(3), 604–615. DOI


Munkemuller, T., Lavergne, S., Bzeznik, B., Dray, S., Jombart, T., Schiffers, K., & Thuiller, W. (2012) — Showed that phylogenetic signal metrics vary in their sensitivity to sample size and tree shape, providing the motivation for testing whether signal estimates are robust to data perturbation. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 3(4), 743–756. DOI

title: Recipe 3: Axis of Diversification
text: When species in my family differ in color pattern, what exactly differs — complexity, orientation, chromatic contrast, or something else?

title: Recipe 3: Axis of Diversification
text: When species in my family differ in color pattern, what exactly differs — complexity, orientation, chromatic contrast, or something else?

title: Recipe 3: Axis of Diversification
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Multivariate ordination / dimensionality reduction



Six pavo variables describe different aspects of color pattern, but they may be correlated — a fish with high transition density (m) probably also has high transition diversity (Jt). Principal component analysis (PCA) finds the independent axes of variation that capture the most variance in the fewest dimensions. Phylogenetic PCA (phyloPCA) does the same thing but accounts for the fact that species are not independent data points: it weights the covariance matrix by the evolutionary relationships encoded in the tree. The result is a low-dimensional summary of how your family’s color patterns actually vary, stripped of the noise introduced by shared ancestry.

title: Recipe 3: Axis of Diversification
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Knowing that color varies is not enough for a poster — you need to know how it varies. Does your family diversify mainly in complexity (busy vs. plain patterns)? In directionality (stripes vs. bars)? In chromatic contrast (vivid vs. muted boundaries)? The phyloPCA biplot answers this by showing which pavo variables load most strongly on each principal component. The dominant axis becomes your family’s headline story: “In this family, the primary axis of color diversification is…”
This recipe produces the hero figure for most posters — a biplot with species plotted in phylogenetic color-pattern space, colored by genus, with loading arrows showing which pavo variables drive each axis.






Clade-specific tips




Pomacanthidae (angelfishes): Expect strong loading of chromatic boundary strength (m_dS) because angelfishes are famous for vivid color contrasts. If m_dS dominates PC1, your poster headline writes itself.
Hypsigenyinae (hogfishes): With ~38 tips, you may find that a single axis captures most of the variance. That is a real result — it means hogfish color diversity is essentially one-dimensional.
Balistoidea: Triggerfishes and filefishes may separate along PC1 or PC2 simply because they belong to different families. If so, the dominant axis is capturing between-family divergence, not within-family diversification.

title: Recipe 3: Axis of Diversification
text:
The Method
Standard PCA finds the directions of maximum variance in a multivariate dataset. Each principal component (PC) is a weighted combination of the original variables. PC1 captures the most variance, PC2 captures the next most (orthogonal to PC1), and so on. The loadings tell you how much each original variable contributes to each PC. A variable with a loading of +0.6 on PC1 pulls species toward the right side of the biplot; a loading of -0.4 pulls them left.
Phylogenetic PCA (phyloPCA), implemented as phytools::phyl.pca(), modifies the centering and covariance calculation by incorporating the tree’s variance-covariance matrix. Under Brownian motion, closely related species are expected to share similar trait values simply because they diverged recently. PhyloPCA removes this expected similarity before extracting principal components, so the resulting axes reflect independent evolutionary changes rather than shared ancestry. The method = "lambda" option estimates the optimal degree of phylogenetic correction via maximum likelihood — it does not assume full Brownian motion but lets the data decide how much tree structure to account for.
The biplot is the key visual output. Species sit as points (colored by genus); loading arrows show which pavo variables drive each axis. Species near each other in the biplot have similar color patterns after accounting for phylogeny. Loading arrows pointing in the same direction indicate correlated pattern features. The proportion of variance explained by each axis (shown on the axis labels) tells you how much of the total color diversity each dimension captures.

title: Recipe 3: Axis of Diversification
text:
How to Interpret Results







Observation
Interpretation




PC1 explains > 50% of variance
Color diversity in your family is effectively one-dimensional. One pavo feature dominates.


PC1 + PC2 together explain > 70%
Two axes capture most of the diversity. Your biplot is a reliable summary.


No single PC exceeds 30%
Color diversity is spread across many dimensions. No single pattern feature dominates — your family diversifies along multiple independent axes.


One loading arrow is much longer than the others on PC1
That variable is the primary axis of diversification. Name it on your poster.


Genera form distinct clusters in the biplot
Color patterns are structured by evolutionary lineage — genera have characteristic color profiles.


Genera overlap heavily
Color patterns have converged across genera, or within-genus variation swamps between-genus differences.









Common pitfalls




Do not interpret phyloPCA axes as “good” or “bad.” PC1 is the axis of maximum variance, not the axis of maximum biological importance. A family could diversify mostly along a dimension that has no ecological significance.
The sign of loadings is arbitrary. If m loads at -0.5 on PC1, that means high-m species sit on the left of the biplot. Flipping all signs gives an equivalent result. Do not read positive = “more” and negative = “less.”
Scaling matters. mode = "corr" (correlation-based PCA) standardizes all variables to equal variance before extracting PCs. This is correct for our data because m (a probability between 0 and 1) and m_dS (a color distance) are on completely different scales. Always use mode = "corr".

title: Recipe 3: Axis of Diversification
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 3: Axis of Diversification ──────────────────────────
source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, ggplot2, theme_poster

# ── 1. Load your bundle and pavo data ──────────────────────────
bundle   <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")
pavo_csv <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# ── 2. Match tree to data ──────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, pavo_csv, species_col = "species")
tree    <- matched$tree
dat     <- matched$data

# ── 3. Build trait matrix ──────────────────────────────────────
pavo_vars <- c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL")
trait_mat <- dat[, pavo_vars]
rownames(trait_mat) <- dat$species

# Drop rows with any NA
complete  <- complete.cases(trait_mat)
trait_mat <- trait_mat[complete, ]
tree_pca  <- ape::drop.tip(tree,
                            setdiff(tree$tip.label, rownames(trait_mat)))
trait_mat <- trait_mat[tree_pca$tip.label, ]   # reorder to match tree

cat("phyloPCA on", nrow(trait_mat), "species x",
    ncol(trait_mat), "variables\n")

# ── 4. Run phyloPCA ───────────────────────────────────────────
phy_pc <- phytools::phyl.pca(tree_pca, trait_mat,
                              method = "lambda", mode = "corr")

# ── 5. Print loadings for PC1–PC3 ─────────────────────────────
cat("\n── Loadings (which variable drives each axis) ──\n")
loadings_mat <- phy_pc$L
print(round(loadings_mat[, 1:min(3, ncol(loadings_mat))], 3))

# Identify the dominant variable on each axis
for (i in 1:min(3, ncol(loadings_mat))) {
  top_var <- names(which.max(abs(loadings_mat[, i])))
  cat(sprintf("  PC%d dominated by: %s (loading = %.3f)\n",
              i, top_var, loadings_mat[top_var, i]))
}

# ── 6. Print variance explained ───────────────────────────────
eigenvalues <- diag(phy_pc$Eval)
var_pct     <- round(100 * eigenvalues / sum(eigenvalues), 1)
cat("\n── Variance explained ──\n")
for (i in seq_along(var_pct)) {
  cat(sprintf("  PC%d: %.1f%%\n", i, var_pct[i]))
}
cat(sprintf("  PC1 + PC2: %.1f%%\n", sum(var_pct[1:2])))

# ── 7. Build the hero biplot ──────────────────────────────────
# Extract scores and add genus labels
scores <- as.data.frame(phy_pc$S[, 1:2])
colnames(scores) <- c("PC1", "PC2")
scores$species <- rownames(scores)
scores$genus   <- sub("_.*", "", scores$species)

# Loading arrows — scale to fit the plot
L <- as.data.frame(loadings_mat[, 1:2])
colnames(L) <- c("PC1", "PC2")
L$variable <- rownames(L)
arrow_scale <- 0.85 *
  min(diff(range(scores$PC1)), diff(range(scores$PC2))) / 2 /
  max(sqrt(L$PC1^2 + L$PC2^2))

p <- ggplot(scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = genus)) +
  # Species points
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.85) +
  # Species labels (abbreviated)
  geom_text(aes(label = sub("^(\\w{4})\\w*_(\\w{4}).*", "\\1_\\2",
                             species)),
            size = 2.8, vjust = -1.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  # Loading arrows
  geom_segment(data = L,
               aes(x = 0, y = 0,
                   xend = PC1 * arrow_scale,
                   yend = PC2 * arrow_scale),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")),
               color = "#c14a4a", linewidth = 1, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # Loading labels
  geom_text(data = L,
            aes(x = PC1 * arrow_scale * 1.15,
                y = PC2 * arrow_scale * 1.15,
                label = variable),
            color = "#c14a4a", fontface = "bold", size = 4.5,
            inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # Axis labels with variance explained
  labs(
    x = sprintf("phyloPC1  (%.1f%% variance)", var_pct[1]),
    y = sprintf("phyloPC2  (%.1f%% variance)", var_pct[2]),
    title = "Axis of color pattern diversification",
    subtitle = "phyloPCA biplot — arrows show pavo variable loadings",
    color = "Genus"
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_poster

print(p)

# ── 8. Save poster-quality PDF ─────────────────────────────────
ggsave("results/recipe3-phylopca-biplot.pdf", p, width = 12, height = 10)
cat("Saved: results/recipe3-phylopca-biplot.pdf\n")

title: Recipe 24: Node Heights Test for Rate Trends
text: Have rates of color pattern evolution accelerated or decelerated through my family’s history?

title: Recipe 24: Node Heights Test for Rate Trends
text: Have rates of color pattern evolution accelerated or decelerated through my family’s history?
crumbs: Recipe 24: Node Heights Test for Rate Trends

title: Recipe 24: Node Heights Test for Rate Trends
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Temporal rate trend detection



The node heights test asks whether the magnitude of evolutionary change is correlated with when that change occurred. It works by computing phylogenetic independent contrasts (PICs) — standardized measures of how much a trait changed at each node — and regressing their absolute values against node age. A significant negative slope means larger changes happened earlier in the tree’s history (deceleration, consistent with early burst or niche filling). A significant positive slope means larger changes happened recently (acceleration). No slope means rates have been constant, consistent with Brownian motion. This is a simple, powerful diagnostic that complements model-based approaches (Recipes 19 and 20) with a regression-based test.
crumbs: Recipe 24: Node Heights Test for Rate Trends

title: Recipe 24: Node Heights Test for Rate Trends
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Model comparison (Recipe 20/22) tells you which evolutionary model best fits the data, but it does not show you the pattern visually. The node heights test produces a scatter plot that makes the temporal trend (or lack of one) immediately visible. A steep negative slope says “the big color changes happened millions of years ago, and recent evolution has been fine-tuning.” A positive slope says “the real action is recent.” Either way, you get a figure that tells a clear story on your poster and complements your DTT (Recipe 19) and model comparison results.






Clade-specific tips




Pomacanthidae (angelfishes): If the deep split between Pomacanthus and Centropyge drove most color divergence, expect a negative slope (deceleration). Recent speciation within Centropyge might involve small color shifts.
Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): Ongoing sexual selection could maintain high rates of color change at recent nodes, producing a flat or positive slope — contrasting with families where color evolution has slowed.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): The deep family-level split should produce a large early contrast. If within-family evolution is modest, expect a clear negative slope.
Hypsigenyinae (hogfishes and allies): With ~38 species, you have relatively few contrasts. The regression may lack power, so report the trend direction even if p > 0.05.
crumbs: Recipe 24: Node Heights Test for Rate Trends

title: Recipe 24: Node Heights Test for Rate Trends
text:
The Method
Phylogenetic independent contrasts (PICs) measure how much a trait changed at each node in the tree, standardized by the expected amount of change given the branch lengths. The absolute value of each contrast tells you the magnitude of evolutionary change at that node, regardless of direction.
The node heights test regresses these absolute contrast values against node ages (measured as time before the present). Under Brownian motion (constant rates), there should be no relationship — the magnitude of change should be the same whether a node is old or young. A significant slope indicates that rates are not constant.
This test was introduced by Freckleton and Harvey (2006) as a diagnostic for non-Brownian evolution in adaptive radiations. It is conceptually simple (just a linear regression), visually intuitive (a scatter plot), and directly interpretable. It is also implemented in the geiger package as nh.test(), but we build it manually here so you can customize the plot for your poster.
crumbs: Recipe 24: Node Heights Test for Rate Trends

title: Recipe 24: Node Heights Test for Rate Trends
text:
How to Interpret Results









Slope
p < 0.05?
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Negative
Yes
Rates decelerated — early burst of color evolution
“The largest color changes occurred early in the family’s history, with rates decelerating toward the present. This is consistent with early ecological or phenotypic niche filling.”


Negative
No
Trend toward deceleration, but not significant
“There is a trend toward early burst, but it is not statistically significant. Rates are consistent with Brownian motion.”


Positive
Yes
Rates accelerated — late burst of color evolution
“Rates of color evolution have increased toward the present, suggesting recent diversification in color is faster than early diversification.”


Positive
No
Trend toward acceleration, but not significant
“There is a non-significant trend toward acceleration, consistent with constant-rate Brownian motion.”


Near zero
No
No temporal trend
“Rates of color evolution show no temporal trend, consistent with constant-rate drift (Brownian motion).”









Common pitfalls




Small sample sizes reduce power. Each internal node produces one contrast, so a tree with N tips gives N-1 contrasts. With fewer than 30 contrasts, the regression may not detect real trends. Report the slope direction even when p > 0.05.
The test assumes contrasts are independent. This is guaranteed by the PIC algorithm when the tree is correct, but violations of the Brownian motion assumption (the very thing you are testing for) can introduce non-independence. Treat this as a diagnostic tool, not a definitive test.
Node ages must be correct. This test requires a time-calibrated (ultrametric) tree. Errors in divergence time estimates will distort the x-axis and can create spurious trends.
Outlier contrasts can drive the regression. A single very large contrast at a deep node can create a significant negative slope even if the rest of the tree is constant-rate. Inspect the scatter plot for influential points.

title: Recipe 24: Node Heights Test for Rate Trends
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 24: Node Heights Test for Rate Trends ──────────────────
source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, ggplot2, theme_poster

# ── 1. Load your tree and pavo data ───────────────────────────────
bundle   <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")
pavo_csv <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# ── 2. Match tree to data ─────────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, pavo_csv, species_col = "species")
tree    <- matched$tree
dat     <- matched$data

cat("Working with", length(tree$tip.label), "species\n")

# ── 3. Check ultrametric ──────────────────────────────────────────
if (!ape::is.ultrametric(tree)) {
  cat("Forcing ultrametric tree (small numerical correction)\n")
  tree <- phytools::force.ultrametric(tree, method = "extend")
}

# ── 4. Node heights test for transition density (m) ───────────────
trait_vec <- setNames(dat$m, dat$species)
trait_vec <- trait_vec[tree$tip.label]

# Compute phylogenetic independent contrasts
contrasts <- pic(trait_vec, tree)

# Get node ages (time from root to each internal node)
node_ages <- branching.times(tree)

# Match contrasts to node ages (both are named by node number)
ages <- node_ages[names(contrasts)]

# Regress |PIC| against node age
model <- lm(abs(contrasts) ~ ages)
s     <- summary(model)

cat("\n── Node Heights Test: transition density (m) ───────────────\n")
cat("Slope:", round(coef(model)[2], 4), "\n")
cat("p-value:", format.pval(s$coefficients[2, 4], digits = 3), "\n")
cat("R-squared:", round(s$r.squared, 3), "\n")

if (coef(model)[2] < 0 && s$coefficients[2, 4] < 0.05) {
  cat("→ Significant DECELERATION: rates were higher early in clade history\n")
} else if (coef(model)[2] > 0 && s$coefficients[2, 4] < 0.05) {
  cat("→ Significant ACCELERATION: rates increased toward the present\n")
} else {
  cat("→ No significant temporal trend in rates\n")
}

# ── 5. Plot ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
pic_df <- data.frame(age = ages, abs_pic = abs(contrasts))

ggplot(pic_df, aes(x = age, y = abs_pic)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.6, color = "#264653") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#e76f51", linewidth = 1.2, se = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Node Heights Test: rate trend through time",
       subtitle = paste0("Slope = ", round(coef(model)[2], 4),
                        ", p = ", format.pval(s$coefficients[2, 4], digits = 3)),
       x = "Node age (millions of years before present)",
       y = "|Phylogenetic independent contrast|") +
  theme_poster

ggsave("results/recipe24-node-heights-m.pdf", width = 8, height = 6)
cat("Saved: results/recipe24-node-heights-m.pdf\n")

# ── 6. Run for all 6 pavo variables ──────────────────────────────
pavo_vars <- c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL")

# Remove species with missing data
complete     <- complete.cases(dat[, pavo_vars])
dat_complete <- dat[complete, ]
tree_sub     <- ape::drop.tip(tree,
                              setdiff(tree$tip.label, dat_complete$species))

nh_summary <- data.frame(
  Variable = character(0),
  Slope    = numeric(0),
  p_value  = numeric(0),
  R_sq     = numeric(0),
  Direction = character(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (v in pavo_vars) {
  x <- setNames(dat_complete[[v]], dat_complete$species)
  x <- x[tree_sub$tip.label]

  con    <- pic(x, tree_sub)
  n_ages <- branching.times(tree_sub)[names(con)]
  mod    <- lm(abs(con) ~ n_ages)
  sm     <- summary(mod)
  sl     <- coef(mod)[2]
  pv     <- sm$coefficients[2, 4]

  direction <- "No trend"
  if (sl < 0 && pv < 0.05) direction <- "Deceleration"
  if (sl > 0 && pv < 0.05) direction <- "Acceleration"

  nh_summary <- rbind(nh_summary, data.frame(
    Variable  = v,
    Slope     = round(sl, 4),
    p_value   = round(pv, 4),
    R_sq      = round(sm$r.squared, 3),
    Direction = direction,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}

cat("\n── Node Heights Test Summary (all 6 pavo variables) ───────\n")
print(nh_summary, row.names = FALSE)

# ── 7. Six-panel scatter plot ─────────────────────────────────────
pdf("results/recipe24-node-heights-all.pdf", width = 12, height = 8)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (v in pavo_vars) {
  x <- setNames(dat_complete[[v]], dat_complete$species)
  x <- x[tree_sub$tip.label]

  con    <- pic(x, tree_sub)
  n_ages <- branching.times(tree_sub)[names(con)]
  mod    <- lm(abs(con) ~ n_ages)
  sm     <- summary(mod)

  plot(n_ages, abs(con),
       pch = 16, col = "#264653", cex = 1.2,
       xlab = "Node age (Myr)", ylab = "|PIC|",
       main = v)
  abline(mod, col = "#e76f51", lwd = 2)
  mtext(paste0("slope=", round(coef(mod)[2], 3),
               " p=", round(sm$coefficients[2, 4], 3)),
        side = 3, line = -1.5, adj = 0.05, cex = 0.8)
}
dev.off()
cat("Saved: results/recipe24-node-heights-all.pdf\n")

title: Recipe 25: ggtree for Publication-Quality Phylogenies
text: How do I make a beautiful, data-rich phylogeny figure with colored branches, tip annotations, clade highlights, and aligned data panels?

title: Recipe 25: ggtree for Publication-Quality Phylogenies
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Phylogenetic data visualization



This is a visualization recipe — it does not test a hypothesis. Instead, it teaches you how to use ggtree, an extension of ggplot2 designed for phylogenetic trees, to produce poster-quality figures that combine tree topology with trait data. ggtree uses the same grammar-of-graphics approach as ggplot2, so if you are comfortable with aes(), geom_*, and theme(), you already know the syntax. The result is a figure that communicates both relationships and trait variation in a single, layered image.

title: Recipe 25: ggtree for Publication-Quality Phylogenies
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Your poster needs at least one phylogeny figure, and it needs to be beautiful. Base R tree plots (from ape::plot.phylo()) work for quick exploration, but they are difficult to customize for a poster. ggtree lets you color branches by trait values, add genus-colored tip points, highlight clades with transparent shading, annotate nodes, and combine the tree with bar charts or heatmaps in multi-panel layouts using patchwork. The figures you produce here will be the visual centerpieces of your poster.






Clade-specific tips




All groups: Start with Recipe E.1 (trait-colored branches) and Recipe E.4 (tree + bar chart). These two layouts work for every family.
Pomacanthidae (angelfishes) and Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): Use the fan layout (Recipe E.2) to display many species compactly, with genus-colored tip points to highlight taxonomic structure.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): Use clade highlighting (Recipe E.3) to visually separate Balistidae from Monacanthidae on the tree.

title: Recipe 25: ggtree for Publication-Quality Phylogenies
text:
The Method
ggtree is a Bioconductor package (not CRAN) that extends ggplot2 to handle phylogenetic tree objects. It converts a tree into a data frame of node coordinates, then plots branches, tips, and annotations as ggplot layers. You can overlay trait data using the %<+% operator, which joins a data frame to the tree by matching tip labels.
This recipe provides four visualization sub-recipes that build on each other:

Trait-colored branches — color each branch by a continuous pavo variable using ancestral state reconstruction to extend values to internal branches.
Fan layout with genus-colored tips — a circular tree with colored tip points, ideal for large trees.
Clade highlighting — shade and label specific clades (genera, subfamilies) on the tree.
Multi-panel: tree + bar chart — combine a phylogeny with an aligned bar chart of trait values using patchwork.







Installing ggtree



ggtree is a Bioconductor package. Install it with:
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("ggtree")
You will also need tidytree (installed automatically with ggtree) and patchwork for multi-panel layouts: install.packages("patchwork").

title: Recipe 25: ggtree for Publication-Quality Phylogenies
text:
How to Interpret the Figure
This is a visualization recipe, not a statistical test. But your figures should reveal:







Visual pattern
What it suggests




Branches shift color at a specific node
A major evolutionary transition in color pattern at that point in the tree


One clade is uniformly one color, another is different
Genus-level or clade-level conservatism in color


Colors are scattered randomly across the tree
Low phylogenetic signal — color is evolutionarily labile


Bar chart heights cluster by clade
Trait values are phylogenetically structured


Bar chart heights are uniform across clades
Trait has converged or is not phylogenetically structured









Common pitfalls




Trait-colored branches require ancestral state estimates. To color internal branches (not just tips), you need ancestral values from fastAnc() (Recipe 23). Without these, only tip branches will have colors.
Fan layout text overlaps. With more than ~50 species, tip labels in fan layout will overlap. Reduce size in geom_tiplab() or use geom_tippoint() alone and add a separate legend.
ggtree objects are ggplots. You can add any ggplot layer (+ theme(), + scale_color_*, etc.). But coord_flip() and coord_polar() do not work with tree layouts — use ggtree’s built-in layout parameter instead.
The %<+% operator is specific to ggtree. It joins a data frame to the tree data by matching the label column (tip labels). Make sure your data frame has a column called label that matches tree$tip.label.

title: Recipe 25: ggtree for Publication-Quality Phylogenies
text:
The Code

Recipe E.1: Trait-colored branches (continuous variable)

# ── Recipe 25.1: Trait-colored branches ───────────────────────────
# Requires: ggtree (Bioconductor), viridis, phytools
# Install ggtree: BiocManager::install("ggtree")

source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, ggplot2, theme_poster
library(ggtree)
library(viridis)

# ── 1. Load tree and pavo data ────────────────────────────────────
bundle   <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")
pavo_csv <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, pavo_csv, species_col = "species")
tree    <- matched$tree
dat     <- matched$data

# ── 2. Prepare trait vector and ancestral estimates ───────────────
trait_vec <- setNames(dat$m, dat$species)
trait_vec <- trait_vec[tree$tip.label]

# Ancestral state reconstruction for internal branches
asr <- fastAnc(tree, trait_vec, CI = TRUE)

# Combine tip and internal node values into one vector
# Node numbering: 1..N = tips, (N+1)..(N+Nnode) = internal
n_tips <- length(tree$tip.label)
all_values <- c(trait_vec[tree$tip.label], asr$ace)

# Build a data frame for ggtree: one row per node
tree_data <- data.frame(
  node  = 1:(n_tips + tree$Nnode),
  value = all_values
)

# ── 3. Plot trait-colored tree ────────────────────────────────────
p <- ggtree(tree, aes(color = value), linewidth = 1.2) %<+% tree_data +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Transition\ndensity (m)",
                        option = "plasma") +
  geom_tiplab(size = 2.5, color = "black", offset = 0.5) +
  theme_tree2() +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.05, 0.85))
p

ggsave("results/recipe25-trait-colored-tree.pdf", p,
       width = 10, height = 12)
cat("Saved: results/recipe25-trait-colored-tree.pdf\n")



Recipe E.2: Fan layout with genus-colored tips

# ── Recipe 25.2: Fan layout with genus-colored tips ───────────────
library(ggtree)

# Build a genus data frame
genus_df <- data.frame(
  label = tree$tip.label,
  genus = sub("_.*", "", tree$tip.label),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

p_fan <- ggtree(tree, layout = "fan", linewidth = 0.8) %<+% genus_df +
  geom_tippoint(aes(color = genus), size = 3) +
  geom_tiplab(aes(color = genus), size = 2, offset = 0.3) +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        legend.text = element_text(face = "italic"))
p_fan

ggsave("results/recipe25-fan-genus-colored.pdf", p_fan,
       width = 12, height = 12)
cat("Saved: results/recipe25-fan-genus-colored.pdf\n")



Recipe E.3: Highlight specific clades

# ── Recipe 25.3: Highlight clades ────────────────────────────────
library(ggtree)

# Start with a simple tree
p_base <- ggtree(tree, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_tiplab(size = 2.5, fontface = "italic")

# Highlight a genus — change "Chaetodon" to a genus in YOUR family
genus_name <- "Chaetodon"   # ← CHANGE THIS to a genus in your tree
genus_tips <- tree$tip.label[grepl(paste0("^", genus_name, "_"),
                                    tree$tip.label)]

if (length(genus_tips) >= 2) {
  mrca <- getMRCA(tree, genus_tips)

  p_highlight <- p_base +
    geom_hilight(node = mrca, fill = "#e9c46a",
                 alpha = 0.2, extend = 5) +
    geom_cladelab(node = mrca, label = genus_name,
                  fontsize = 5, offset = 3, barsize = 1.5,
                  color = "#e9c46a", fontface = "italic")
  p_highlight

  ggsave("results/recipe25-clade-highlight.pdf", p_highlight,
         width = 10, height = 12)
  cat("Saved: results/recipe25-clade-highlight.pdf\n")
} else {
  cat("Need at least 2 species in genus '", genus_name,
      "' to highlight a clade.\n")
  cat("Change genus_name to a genus with multiple species in your tree.\n")
}



Recipe E.4: Multi-panel — tree + bar chart

# ── Recipe 25.4: Multi-panel tree + bar chart ─────────────────────
# Requires: patchwork
# If not installed: install.packages("patchwork")

library(ggtree)
library(patchwork)

# ── Left panel: phylogeny ─────────────────────────────────────────
p_tree <- ggtree(tree, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_tiplab(size = 2.5, fontface = "italic")

# ── Right panel: bar chart of transition density ──────────────────
# IMPORTANT: species order must match the tree tip order in the plot
# get_taxa_name() extracts tips in the order they appear in the ggtree plot
tip_order <- rev(get_taxa_name(p_tree))

trait_bar <- data.frame(
  species = tree$tip.label,
  m       = trait_vec[tree$tip.label],
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
trait_bar$species <- factor(trait_bar$species, levels = tip_order)

p_bar <- ggplot(trait_bar, aes(x = m, y = species)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a9d8f", alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(x = "Transition density (m)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())

# ── Combine with patchwork ────────────────────────────────────────
combined <- p_tree + p_bar + plot_layout(widths = c(3, 1))
combined

ggsave("results/recipe25-tree-plus-bar.pdf", combined,
       width = 12, height = max(8, length(tree$tip.label) * 0.3))
cat("Saved: results/recipe25-tree-plus-bar.pdf\n")
