title: Recipe: Tree with Species Images
text: Plot your phylogenetic tree with species photographs at each tip, labeled with italic binomials — in both rectangular and circular (fan) layouts.

title: Recipe: Tree with Species Images
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Every group has exemplar images from FishView. Plotting them on the tree immediately reveals whether similar-looking species are close relatives (phylogenetic signal in appearance) or scattered across the tree (convergence). This figure also shows your audience the organisms before you hit them with statistics.






Parrotfish and wrasse groups



Your images are mostly terminal-phase males. Plotting them on the tree makes the IP/TP color difference vivid — if you have any IP images mixed in, they’ll stand out immediately as the drab outliers.

title: Recipe: Tree with Species Images
text:
The Method
This recipe uses base R phylogenetic plotting (ape::plot.phylo()) with rasterImage() to overlay PNG images at tip coordinates. No special packages beyond ape, phytools, and png are needed.
The approach:

Load and normalize the tree (strip specimen codes to clean Genus_species)
Find the exemplar image for each species in the bundle’s images/ directory
Plot the tree without tip labels
Overlay each species’ photo at its tip position
Add an italic species name below each image

We show two layouts: rectangular (best for posters where you need to read species names) and fan/circle (best for showing many species compactly).

title: Recipe: Tree with Species Images
text:
How to Interpret the Figure
This is a visualization recipe, not a statistical test. But look for:







Pattern
What it suggests




Similar-looking species clustered together
Color pattern has phylogenetic signal — close relatives look alike


Similar colors scattered across the tree
Convergent evolution — distantly related species evolved similar appearances


One subclade looks dramatically different
Possible adaptive radiation in color, or a shift in ecology/habitat


Obvious outlier (drab among colorful)
May be a juvenile or IP individual mixed into your dataset — check it

title: Recipe: Tree with Species Images
text:
The Code

Setup: Load packages and prepare the tree

library(ape)
library(phytools)
library(png)

# ── 1. Load and normalize the tree ──────────────────────────────
# Point this to YOUR bundle directory
bundle_dir <- "path/to/your/bundle"

# Find the tree file
tree_file <- list.files(bundle_dir, pattern = "-mini-tree\\.tre$",
                        full.names = TRUE)[1]
tree <- tryCatch(read.nexus(tree_file),
                 error = function(e) read.tree(tree_file))
if (inherits(tree, "multiPhylo")) tree <- tree[[1]]

# Normalize tip labels to Genus_species (strip specimen codes)
to_binomial <- function(tips) {
  vapply(tips, function(t) {
    parts <- strsplit(t, "_", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
    if (length(parts) < 2) return(parts[1])
    genus   <- parts[1]
    species <- sub("^([a-z]+).*", "\\1", parts[2])
    paste(genus, species, sep = "_")
  }, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
}

tree$tip.label <- to_binomial(tree$tip.label)

# Drop duplicate tips (keeps first occurrence)
dups <- duplicated(tree$tip.label)
if (any(dups)) tree <- drop.tip(tree, tree$tip.label[dups])

# ── 2. Prune to species with images ────────────────────────────
img_dir <- file.path(bundle_dir, "images")
# Each species has a subdirectory with exemplar.png
img_species <- basename(list.dirs(img_dir, recursive = FALSE))

# Keep only species that are in BOTH the tree AND the image directory
keep <- intersect(tree$tip.label, img_species)
cat(length(keep), "species with both tree tip and image\n")

tree_img <- drop.tip(tree, setdiff(tree$tip.label, keep))

# ── 3. Build a named list of image paths ───────────────────────
img_paths <- setNames(
  file.path(img_dir, tree_img$tip.label, "exemplar.png"),
  tree_img$tip.label
)

# Check all exist
missing <- names(img_paths)[!file.exists(img_paths)]
if (length(missing) > 0) {
  cat("Warning: no exemplar.png for:", paste(missing, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  img_paths <- img_paths[file.exists(img_paths)]
  tree_img <- drop.tip(tree_img, missing)
}



Rectangular tree with images

# ── 4a. Rectangular tree with images ───────────────────────────

n_tips     <- length(tree_img$tip.label)
tree_depth <- max(node.depth.edgelength(tree_img))

# Reserve right side for images
x_max <- tree_depth * 1.65

# Plot the tree (no tip labels — we'll add them under the images)
par(mar = c(2, 1, 3, 1), xpd = NA)
plot(tree_img,
     show.tip.label = FALSE,
     no.margin = FALSE,
     x.lim = c(0, x_max),
     y.lim = c(0.5, n_tips + 0.5),
     edge.width = 2.5,
     edge.color = "#333333")
title(main = "Your family on the tree", cex.main = 1.4)

# Get tip coordinates from the last plot
pp <- get("last_plot.phylo", envir = .PlotPhyloEnv)

# Image sizing
img_h <- min(0.85, 0.9 * max(1, 3 / n_tips))   # height in tip-row units
img_w <- 0.35 * tree_depth                       # width in tree-depth units
x_left <- tree_depth + 0.04 * tree_depth         # small gap past branch tips
x_right <- x_left + img_w

# Overlay images and labels
for (i in seq_along(tree_img$tip.label)) {
  tip <- tree_img$tip.label[i]
  if (!(tip %in% names(img_paths))) next

  img <- readPNG(img_paths[tip])
  tip_y <- pp$yy[i]

  rasterImage(img,
              xleft = x_left,
              ybottom = tip_y - img_h / 2,
              xright = x_right,
              ytop = tip_y + img_h / 2,
              interpolate = TRUE)

  # Italic species name below the image
  label <- gsub("_", " ", tip)
  text(x = (x_left + x_right) / 2,
       y = tip_y - img_h / 2 - 0.08,
       labels = label,
       font = 3, cex = 0.7, adj = c(0.5, 1))
}



Fan (circle) tree with images

# ── 4b. Fan (circle) tree with images ─────────────────────────

# For a fan layout, images are placed radially around the tree.
# We use phytools::plotTree with type="fan" and manually compute
# polar coordinates for each image.

par(mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1), xpd = NA)
plot(tree_img,
     type = "fan",
     show.tip.label = FALSE,
     no.margin = FALSE,
     edge.width = 2.5,
     edge.color = "#333333",
     open.angle = 10)     # small gap at the bottom
title(main = "Your family — fan layout", cex.main = 1.4)

# Get tip coordinates (these are already in Cartesian x,y for the fan)
pp <- get("last_plot.phylo", envir = .PlotPhyloEnv)

# Image size in plot units — scale relative to the tree radius
tree_radius <- max(sqrt(pp$xx^2 + pp$yy^2))
img_size <- tree_radius * 0.12   # adjust this to change image size

for (i in seq_along(tree_img$tip.label)) {
  tip <- tree_img$tip.label[i]
  if (!(tip %in% names(img_paths))) next

  img <- readPNG(img_paths[tip])

  # Tip position in the fan
  tx <- pp$xx[i]
  ty <- pp$yy[i]

  # Push image outward from the tip along the radial direction
  angle <- atan2(ty, tx)
  offset <- tree_radius * 0.08   # gap between branch tip and image
  cx <- tx + cos(angle) * offset
  cy <- ty + sin(angle) * offset

  # Aspect ratio of the image
  asp <- ncol(img) / nrow(img)
  half_w <- img_size * asp / 2
  half_h <- img_size / 2

  rasterImage(img,
              xleft   = cx - half_w,
              ybottom = cy - half_h,
              xright  = cx + half_w,
              ytop    = cy + half_h,
              interpolate = TRUE)

  # Species label below the image (slightly further out)
  label <- gsub("_", " ", tip)
  label_r <- offset + img_size * 1.1
  lx <- tx + cos(angle) * label_r
  ly <- ty + sin(angle) * label_r

  # Rotate text to follow the angle (readable orientation)
  angle_deg <- angle * 180 / pi
  adj <- if (abs(angle_deg) > 90) c(1, 0.5) else c(0, 0.5)
  if (abs(angle_deg) > 90) angle_deg <- angle_deg + 180

  text(lx, ly, labels = label,
       srt = angle_deg, font = 3, cex = 0.55, adj = adj)
}



Save as PDF

# ── 5. Save as PDF ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# Rectangular tree
pdf("tree-rectangular.pdf", width = 14, height = max(8, n_tips * 0.5))
# ... paste the rectangular plotting code from above here ...
dev.off()
cat("Saved: tree-rectangular.pdf\n")

# Fan tree
pdf("tree-fan.pdf", width = 14, height = 14)
# ... paste the fan plotting code from above here ...
dev.off()
cat("Saved: tree-fan.pdf\n")

# Tip: for poster figures, use width = 14 and a large height.
# PDF is vector format — it scales perfectly at any size.







Poster tip



The rectangular layout works best when you have fewer than ~25 species (the images stay large enough to see). For 30+ species, use the fan layout — it packs more species into the same space. Export as PDF for perfect scaling on your poster.

title: Recipe: Tree with Species Images
text:
Worked Example: Chaetodontidae
Here is the complete code to produce both trees from the Chaetodontidae mini-bundle (the Demo 8 walkthrough dataset). You can run this as-is to test the recipe before adapting it to your own clade.

# ── Worked example: Chaetodontidae butterflyfishes ─────────────
library(ape)
library(phytools)
library(png)

bundle_dir <- "path/to/chaetodontidae-mini-bundle"  # ← update this path

# Load tree
tree_file <- list.files(bundle_dir, pattern = "-mini-tree\\.tre$",
                        full.names = TRUE)[1]
tree <- read.tree(tree_file)
if (inherits(tree, "multiPhylo")) tree <- tree[[1]]

# Normalize tips
to_binomial <- function(tips) {
  vapply(tips, function(t) {
    parts <- strsplit(t, "_", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
    if (length(parts) < 2) return(parts[1])
    paste(parts[1], sub("^([a-z]+).*", "\\1", parts[2]), sep = "_")
  }, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
}
tree$tip.label <- to_binomial(tree$tip.label)
dups <- duplicated(tree$tip.label)
if (any(dups)) tree <- drop.tip(tree, tree$tip.label[dups])

# Find species with images
img_dir <- file.path(bundle_dir, "images")
img_species <- basename(list.dirs(img_dir, recursive = FALSE))
keep <- intersect(tree$tip.label, img_species)
tree_img <- drop.tip(tree, setdiff(tree$tip.label, keep))

img_paths <- setNames(
  file.path(img_dir, tree_img$tip.label, "exemplar.png"),
  tree_img$tip.label
)
# Drop any without exemplar.png (e.g., error-species with only img-1..5)
exists_mask <- file.exists(img_paths)
if (!all(exists_mask)) {
  cat("Skipping (no exemplar.png):", paste(names(img_paths)[!exists_mask], collapse=", "), "\n")
  img_paths <- img_paths[exists_mask]
  tree_img <- drop.tip(tree_img, setdiff(tree_img$tip.label, names(img_paths)))
}

n_tips <- length(tree_img$tip.label)
tree_depth <- max(node.depth.edgelength(tree_img))
cat(n_tips, "butterflyfishes with images on tree\n")

# ── Rectangular PDF ──
pdf("chaet-tree-rectangular.pdf", width = 14, height = max(8, n_tips * 0.55))
x_max <- tree_depth * 1.65
par(mar = c(2, 1, 3, 1), xpd = NA)
plot(tree_img, show.tip.label = FALSE, no.margin = FALSE,
     x.lim = c(0, x_max), y.lim = c(0.5, n_tips + 0.5),
     edge.width = 2.5, edge.color = "#333333")
title("Chaetodontidae — rectangular tree with images", cex.main = 1.4)
pp <- get("last_plot.phylo", envir = .PlotPhyloEnv)
img_h <- min(0.85, 0.9 * max(1, 3 / n_tips))
img_w <- 0.35 * tree_depth
x_left <- tree_depth + 0.04 * tree_depth
x_right <- x_left + img_w
for (i in seq_along(tree_img$tip.label)) {
  tip <- tree_img$tip.label[i]
  img <- readPNG(img_paths[tip])
  tip_y <- pp$yy[i]
  rasterImage(img, x_left, tip_y - img_h/2, x_right, tip_y + img_h/2,
              interpolate = TRUE)
  text((x_left + x_right)/2, tip_y - img_h/2 - 0.08,
       gsub("_", " ", tip), font = 3, cex = 0.7, adj = c(0.5, 1))
}
dev.off()
cat("Saved: chaet-tree-rectangular.pdf\n")

# ── Fan PDF ──
pdf("chaet-tree-fan.pdf", width = 14, height = 14)
par(mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1), xpd = NA)
plot(tree_img, type = "fan", show.tip.label = FALSE, no.margin = FALSE,
     edge.width = 2.5, edge.color = "#333333", open.angle = 10)
title("Chaetodontidae — fan tree with images", cex.main = 1.4)
pp <- get("last_plot.phylo", envir = .PlotPhyloEnv)
tree_radius <- max(sqrt(pp$xx^2 + pp$yy^2))
img_size <- tree_radius * 0.12
for (i in seq_along(tree_img$tip.label)) {
  tip <- tree_img$tip.label[i]
  img <- readPNG(img_paths[tip])
  tx <- pp$xx[i]; ty <- pp$yy[i]
  angle <- atan2(ty, tx)
  offset <- tree_radius * 0.08
  cx <- tx + cos(angle) * offset
  cy <- ty + sin(angle) * offset
  asp <- ncol(img) / nrow(img)
  half_w <- img_size * asp / 2; half_h <- img_size / 2
  rasterImage(img, cx - half_w, cy - half_h, cx + half_w, cy + half_h,
              interpolate = TRUE)
  label <- gsub("_", " ", tip)
  label_r <- offset + img_size * 1.1
  lx <- tx + cos(angle) * label_r
  ly <- ty + sin(angle) * label_r
  angle_deg <- angle * 180 / pi
  adj <- if (abs(angle_deg) > 90) c(1, 0.5) else c(0, 0.5)
  if (abs(angle_deg) > 90) angle_deg <- angle_deg + 180
  text(lx, ly, label, srt = angle_deg, font = 3, cex = 0.55, adj = adj)
}
dev.off()
cat("Saved: chaet-tree-fan.pdf\n")

title: Recipe 14: Schooling and Conspicuousness
text: Do schooling reef fish species have more uniform, less individually distinctive color patterns than solitary species — or do they actually show higher conspicuousness, consistent with school membership relaxing the need for individual crypsis?

title: Recipe 14: Schooling and Conspicuousness
text: Do schooling reef fish species have more uniform, less individually distinctive color patterns than solitary species — or do they actually show higher conspicuousness, consistent with school membership relaxing the need for individual crypsis?

title: Recipe 14: Schooling and Conspicuousness
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Categorical PGLS — testing whether a discrete behavioral ecology state predicts a continuous color metric



You are asking whether the ecological strategy of group living predicts color pattern metrics after accounting for shared ancestry. This is a one-way phylogenetic ANOVA (PGLS with a binary categorical predictor). The question is genuinely two-directional: theory generates competing predictions, and finding either outcome is interpretable and interesting. The recipe below tests m_dS (achromatic contrast, relevant to the brightness-based confusion effect) and Jc (chromatic complexity) against a binary schooling variable pulled from FishBase’s ecology table.

title: Recipe 14: Schooling and Conspicuousness
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Schooling behavior creates two opposing selective pressures on individual color patterns:
The confusion effect (favoring conspicuousness): A dense, moving school presents predators with many identical targets and overwhelms their ability to track one individual. Individual conspicuousness — even high contrast — may be tolerated or even favored if it helps the school cohere and coordinate, making the confusion effect stronger.
The oddity effect (favoring uniformity): A phenotypically odd individual stands out from its schoolmates and becomes a disproportionate target for predators seeking a trackable individual. This selects for extreme homogeneity within schools — and could mean schooling species evolve lower pattern complexity or lower individual distinctiveness than solitary species.
Which effect dominates varies by group, predator type, and the scale of the pattern relative to viewing distance. Testing this across your clade tells you something about which of these ecological forces has had a stronger hand in shaping color evolution.






Clade-specific tips




Acanthuridae (surgeonfishes): This family includes species that school intensely (many Acanthurus, Ctenochaetus) alongside distinctly solitary or pair-territorial species (Zebrasoma, some Naso). Within-family contrast is strong, making this an ideal group for Recipe 14.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): Most triggerfishes are solitary and territorial, while a few filefish species can be found in loose aggregations. Sample sizes in each category may be small — check before committing.
Scarinae (parrotfishes): Some species feed in small loose groups, others are more solitary or harem-based. FishBase Schooling codes can be sparse for this group; check coverage before running the recipe.
Pomacanthidae (angelfishes): Largely solitary or pair-living; “schooling” records are rare. This recipe may not be well-powered for angelfishes specifically.
Cirrhilabrini / Halichoerinae / Hypsigenyinae: Moderate to good FishBase coverage. Worth trying especially for genera that span both habits.

title: Recipe 14: Schooling and Conspicuousness
text:
The Method
You will pull the ecology table from FishBase for your species, extract the Schooling column, and collapse it into a binary predictor: schooling versus solitary/pairs. Species coded as “aggregating,” “loose groups,” or similar intermediate categories may need manual review — print the raw values and decide how to bin them before running the model.
The primary PGLS tests m_dS ~ schooling_binary. Achromatic contrast (m_dS) is the metric most directly relevant to the confusion-effect prediction because the dazzle effect of schooling depends on high-contrast body markings that are visible to predators across viewing distances, and predator luminance channels (green-shifted in many teleosts) are most sensitive to this axis. You can also run Jc ~ schooling_binary as a secondary test of chromatic conspicuousness.

title: Recipe 14: Schooling and Conspicuousness
text:
How to Interpret Results








Result
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Schooling m_dS > solitary m_dS, p < 0.05
Schooling species have more achromatic contrast
“Schooling species show higher achromatic contrast, consistent with high-contrast stripe patterns facilitating school cohesion or dazzle-based predator confusion.”


Schooling m_dS < solitary m_dS, p < 0.05
Schooling species have less achromatic contrast
“Schooling species show lower contrast patterns, potentially reflecting the oddity effect: uniform-looking individuals are less likely to be singled out by predators.”


No significant difference, p > 0.05
Schooling behavior does not predict achromatic contrast
“We find no significant relationship between schooling behavior and achromatic contrast in our clade, suggesting color pattern may be shaped more strongly by diet or habitat than by social behavior.”


Schooling Jc > solitary Jc, p < 0.05
Schooling species are more chromatically complex
“Chromatic complexity is elevated in schooling species; this may reflect species recognition signals that help fish identify and join conspecific schools.”









Common pitfalls




FishBase “Schooling” is a coarse field. It distinguishes schooling, aggregating, and solitary/pairs, but the boundary between “schooling” and “aggregating” is not always consistently applied across families. Print table(merged$Schooling, useNA = "always") before cleaning and look for unexpected entries.
“Schooling” in FishBase often refers to larvae or juveniles. Many reef fish school as larvae or small juveniles even if adults are solitary. If you can, try to verify whether the FishBase entry refers to adult behavior.
Low FishBase coverage for some clades. If more than 30% of your species return NA for Schooling, the cleaned binary sample will be small and potentially biased toward well-studied species. Report coverage explicitly.
The confusion and oddity effects may operate at different spatial scales. High-contrast horizontal stripes (like surgeonfish) could simultaneously create school-level dazzle (high m_dS within school) AND individual oddity risk if one fish in the school lacks stripes. Your PGLS tests the between-species level, not the within-school effect — keep this distinction clear in your interpretation.

title: Recipe 14: Schooling and Conspicuousness
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 14: Schooling and Conspicuousness ─────────────────────
source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, nlme, ggplot2, theme_poster

# ── 1. Load your pavo metrics and tree ──────────────────────────
traits <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
tree   <- ape::read.tree("path/to/your-family-mini-tree.tre")

# ── 2. Pull schooling behavior from FishBase ─────────────────────
fb <- pull_fishbase(traits$species,
                    fields = list(ecology = c("Schooling")))

cat("Raw Schooling values from FishBase:\n")
print(table(fb$Schooling, useNA = "always"))

# ── 3. Merge and clean to binary predictor ──────────────────────
merged <- merge(traits, fb, by = "species")

# Collapse to "schooling" vs "solitary_pairs"
# Review the raw table above and adjust regex if needed for your clade
merged$schooling_binary <- ifelse(
  grepl("school", merged$Schooling, ignore.case = TRUE),
  "schooling",
  ifelse(
    grepl("solitar|pair|alone|non-school", merged$Schooling,
          ignore.case = TRUE),
    "solitary_pairs",
    NA
  )
)

cat("\nSpecies retained by schooling category:\n")
print(table(merged$schooling_binary, useNA = "always"))

# Drop species with NA or ambiguous schooling status
n_before <- nrow(merged)
merged   <- merged[!is.na(merged$schooling_binary), ]
cat("\nDropped", n_before - nrow(merged),
    "species with NA or ambiguous schooling\n")

title: Recipe 8: Diet and Conspicuousness
text: Does trophic level predict how chromatically conspicuous a species is — and if so, which direction does the relationship go?

title: Recipe 8: Diet and Conspicuousness
text: Does trophic level predict how chromatically conspicuous a species is — and if so, which direction does the relationship go?

title: Recipe 8: Diet and Conspicuousness
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Ecological niche and signal evolution



This recipe tests whether a species’ position in the food web predicts its visual signaling strategy. Diet is a fundamental ecological axis that determines foraging behavior, social structure, and exposure to predators. Herbivores, planktivores, and carnivores face different selection pressures on coloration: an ambush predator may need crypsis, while a territorial herbivore may benefit from conspicuous species-recognition signals. Testing this with PGLS asks whether these pressures leave a detectable evolutionary signature across your clade.

title: Recipe 8: Diet and Conspicuousness
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Trophic level (Troph in FishBase) is a continuous variable ranging from about 2.0 (strict herbivores/detritivores) to 4.5+ (top predators). Unlike categorical diet labels, Troph is estimated from quantitative stomach content or stable isotope data, making it suitable for regression. The prediction is not straightforward: you might expect high-trophic carnivores to be less conspicuous (ambush predation favors crypsis), but many reef carnivores are brightly colored (think lionfish or groupers). Conversely, herbivorous surgeonfishes and parrotfishes are often boldly colored, possibly because their algal diet provides carotenoid pigments and their social structure favors species recognition. Your data will tell you which story holds for your clade.






Clade-specific tips




Acanthuridae (surgeonfishes): This family spans a wide trophic range: Naso species include planktivores (high Troph), while Zebrasoma and Acanthurus include strict algal grazers (low Troph). Both extremes include strikingly colored species — testing whether the relationship is flat would itself be interesting.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): Varied diets from sponge-eaters to hard-shelled invertebrate specialists. Triggerfishes are often boldly patterned regardless of diet, which could indicate that diet does not constrain coloration in this group.
Labridae (wrasses): Enormous trophic diversity, from coral-feeding Labrichthys to piscivorous Cheilinus. The broad range should give good statistical power.

title: Recipe 8: Diet and Conspicuousness
text:
The Method
We use PGLS to regress chromatic contrast (m_dS) against trophic level (Troph). No log transform is needed for Troph because it is already on a bounded, approximately linear scale (~2 to ~4.5). Chromatic contrast (m_dS) measures the average difference in saturation between adjacent color pattern elements — higher values mean more chromatically conspicuous patterns. PGLS accounts for phylogeny so that the result is not driven by, for example, all the conspicuous species being in one clade that happens to be herbivorous.
Consider also running this analysis with m_dL (achromatic/luminance contrast) as the dependent variable. Some species may be cryptic in hue but highly contrasting in brightness, or vice versa. Comparing the two results adds depth to your poster.

title: Recipe 8: Diet and Conspicuousness
text:
How to Interpret Results








Result
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Negative slope, p < 0.05
Higher trophic level (more carnivorous) = less conspicuous
“Carnivorous species in [family] are significantly less chromatically conspicuous than herbivores, consistent with selection for crypsis in predatory species.”


Positive slope, p < 0.05
Higher trophic level = more conspicuous
“Carnivorous species in [family] are more chromatically conspicuous. This could reflect honest signaling of predator status, or a release from herbivore-specific constraints.”


p > 0.05
No significant relationship
“Trophic level does not predict chromatic conspicuousness in [family] after controlling for phylogeny. Color signals may serve functions (mate choice, species recognition) that are independent of feeding ecology.”









Common pitfalls




Troph is an estimate, not a direct measurement. FishBase Troph values are computed from diet composition data using a standardized algorithm. Accuracy varies by species — well-studied species have better estimates. Check the number of diet studies underlying each estimate if precision concerns you.
Trophic level conflates diet type with diet breadth. A specialist corallivore and a generalist omnivore might have similar Troph values but very different ecologies. If your clade has complex trophic structure, consider also looking at diet composition categories from the ecology() table.
Consider size correction (Recipe 7b). Body size correlates with both trophic level (larger fish tend to be more carnivorous) and color. Run Recipe 7b first if you suspect size is a confound.

title: Recipe 8: Diet and Conspicuousness
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 8: Diet and Conspicuousness ────────────────────────
source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")

# ── 1. Load your data ────────────────────────────────────────
traits <- read.csv("path/to/your/pavo_metrics.csv",
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
bundle <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")

# ── 2. Pull trophic level from FishBase ──────────────────────
fb <- pull_fishbase(traits$species,
                    fields = list(estimate = c("Troph")))

# ── 3. Merge ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
merged <- merge(traits, fb, by = "species")
merged <- merged[!is.na(merged$Troph), ]

cat("Species with trophic data:", nrow(merged), "\n")
cat("Troph range:", round(range(merged$Troph), 2), "\n")

# ── 4. Match to tree ────────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, merged, species_col = "species")

# ── 5. PGLS: chromatic contrast vs trophic level ────────────
model <- safe_pgls(m_dS ~ Troph, df = matched$data, tree = matched$tree)

# ── 6. Scatter plot ─────────────────────────────────────────
library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(matched$data, aes(x = Troph, y = m_dS)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.7, color = "#264653") +
  { if (!is.null(model))
    geom_abline(intercept = coef(model)[1], slope = coef(model)[2],
                color = "#e76f51", linewidth = 1.2) } +
  labs(x = "Trophic Level (Troph)",
       y = "Mean Chromatic Contrast (m_dS)",
       title = "Does diet predict conspicuousness?",
       subtitle = "PGLS controlling for phylogeny") +
  theme_poster

print(p)
ggsave("results/recipe8-diet-vs-conspicuousness.pdf", p,
       width = 10, height = 8)
cat("Saved: results/recipe8-diet-vs-conspicuousness.pdf\n")

title: Recipe 8: Diet and Conspicuousness
text:
From the Literature

Endler, J. A. (1978) — The foundational paper on predator perception and animal color patterns, demonstrating that guppy color patterns represent a compromise between sexual selection (favoring conspicuousness) and predation pressure (favoring crypsis). The framework applies broadly to any system where diet-related ecology creates differential predation regimes. Evolutionary Biology, 11, 319–364.


Marshall, N. J. (2000) — Showed that reef fish use the same “bright” colors for both communication and camouflage, depending on viewing distance and background. This challenges simple predictions about diet and conspicuousness: a species can be simultaneously conspicuous to conspecifics at short range and cryptic to predators at long range. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 355(1401), 1243–1248. DOI

title: Recipe 11: Swimming Mode and Pattern
text: Does swimming performance, as reflected in caudal fin shape, predict the spatial organization of color patterns — and could fast-moving species benefit from motion dazzle?

title: Recipe 11: Swimming Mode and Pattern
text: Does swimming performance, as reflected in caudal fin shape, predict the spatial organization of color patterns — and could fast-moving species benefit from motion dazzle?

title: Recipe 11: Swimming Mode and Pattern
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Locomotion and visual signal co-evolution



This recipe tests whether the biomechanics of movement influence the evolution of static color patterns. A high-aspect-ratio caudal fin indicates sustained fast swimming (cruising), while a low-aspect-ratio fin indicates maneuvering or burst swimming. If color patterns interact with motion to create visual effects — such as motion dazzle, where stripes confuse a predator’s ability to track speed and direction — then we should see a correlation between fin shape and pattern geometry. This connects locomotor ecology to the visual ecology of anti-predator defense.

title: Recipe 11: Swimming Mode and Pattern
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
The “motion dazzle” hypothesis (covered in Lecture 14) proposes that high-contrast stripes and geometric patterns can disrupt a predator’s ability to accurately judge the speed, direction, or trajectory of a moving target. If this mechanism operates in reef fishes, species that are frequently in motion (cruisers with high caudal fin aspect ratio) should have different pattern properties than sit-and-wait or reef-associated species with low aspect ratios. Specifically, we might predict that fast swimmers have higher pattern aspect ratio (A from pavo, which captures pattern elongation/orientation) or different spatial frequency distributions.
Alternatively, the relationship could go the other direction: species that rely on sustained swimming may benefit more from streamlined, low-contrast coloration that reduces conspicuousness during constant movement, while reef-associated maneuverers invest in bold patterns for territorial signaling at close range.






Clade-specific tips




Acanthuridae (surgeonfishes): Include both reef-cruisers (Naso, high caudal AR) and territorial reef-dwellers (Zebrasoma, lower caudal AR). The tightly schooling Naso species often have more uniform coloration, while territorial Zebrasoma have bold patterns — consistent with a motion-pattern link.
Labridae (wrasses): Most wrasses are pectoral-fin swimmers (labriform locomotion) rather than caudal-fin swimmers, so caudal AR may be less biologically meaningful. Consider whether pectoral fin aspect ratio (not currently in FishBase) would be a better predictor for this family.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): Use undulatory locomotion (dorsal + anal fin propulsion) rather than caudal fin propulsion. Caudal fin AR may not reflect their actual swimming mode — note this caveat.

title: Recipe 11: Swimming Mode and Pattern
text:
The Method
We use PGLS to regress the pavo pattern aspect ratio (A) against the FishBase caudal fin aspect ratio (AspectRatio from the morphometrics() table). The pavo metric A captures the degree of pattern elongation and orientation: high A indicates horizontally or vertically elongated pattern elements (stripes), while low A indicates uniform or isotropic patterns. The FishBase AspectRatio measures caudal fin shape: high values indicate lunate, crescent-shaped fins associated with sustained fast swimming, while low values indicate rounded fins associated with maneuverability.






Why morphometrics() and not estimate()?



In older rfishbase (≤ 3.x) AspectRatio was exposed through estimate(). From rfishbase 5.x onward it lives in the morphometrics() table, which often returns multiple measurements per species. pull_fishbase() aggregates by taking the first record per species so you get one row per species back.


The motion dazzle prediction is that species with high caudal AR (fast cruisers) should have high pattern A (striped, directional patterns). An alternative prediction is that fast swimmers have low pattern A (uniform coloration for low conspicuousness during movement). Your data will distinguish between these hypotheses for your clade.

title: Recipe 11: Swimming Mode and Pattern
text:
How to Interpret Results








Result
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Positive slope, p < 0.05
Fast swimmers have more directional patterns
“Fast-swimming species in [family] have more elongated pattern elements, consistent with the motion dazzle hypothesis — stripes on a moving body may confuse predator tracking.”


Negative slope, p < 0.05
Fast swimmers have more uniform patterns
“Fast-swimming species have less directional patterning, suggesting that sustained locomotion favors streamlined visual profiles rather than dazzle camouflage.”


p > 0.05
No significant relationship
“Swimming mode does not predict pattern orientation in [family]. Color pattern geometry may be shaped by other ecological pressures (territoriality, mate choice) rather than locomotor ecology.”









Common pitfalls




Caudal fin AR is only relevant for caudal-fin swimmers. Many reef fish families (wrasses, triggerfishes, boxfishes) use non-caudal propulsion. For these groups, the caudal fin AR may not reflect actual swimming mode. Acknowledge this in your poster.
The motion dazzle hypothesis is about moving targets viewed by predators. Your pavo measurements are from static images. A species could have high pattern A (stripes) for reasons unrelated to motion — e.g., social signaling, species recognition, or disruptive coloration while stationary.
pavo’s A (aspect ratio of pattern) and FishBase’s AspectRatio (caudal fin shape) are completely different measurements. Label your axes clearly to avoid confusion. Consider using “pattern AR” and “caudal fin AR” in your text.

title: Recipe 11: Swimming Mode and Pattern
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 11: Swimming Mode and Pattern ──────────────────────
source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")

# ── 1. Load your data ────────────────────────────────────────
traits <- read.csv("path/to/your/pavo_metrics.csv",
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
bundle <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")

# ── 2. Pull caudal fin aspect ratio from FishBase ────────────
# Note: AspectRatio lives in morphometrics() in rfishbase 5.x
# (it was in estimate() in older versions). pull_fishbase() returns
# one row per species (first measurement) for downstream merging.
fb <- pull_fishbase(traits$species,
                    fields = list(morphometrics = c("AspectRatio")))

# ── 3. Merge ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
merged <- merge(traits, fb, by = "species")
merged <- merged[!is.na(merged$AspectRatio) & merged$AspectRatio > 0, ]

cat("Species with caudal fin AR data:", nrow(merged), "\n")
cat("Caudal AR range:", round(range(merged$AspectRatio), 2), "\n")

# ── 4. Match to tree ────────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, merged, species_col = "species")

# ── 5. PGLS: pattern aspect ratio vs caudal fin AR ──────────
model <- safe_pgls(A ~ AspectRatio, df = matched$data, tree = matched$tree)

# ── 6. Scatter plot ─────────────────────────────────────────
library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(matched$data, aes(x = AspectRatio, y = A)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.7, color = "#264653") +
  { if (!is.null(model))
    geom_abline(intercept = coef(model)[1], slope = coef(model)[2],
                color = "#e76f51", linewidth = 1.2) } +
  labs(x = "Caudal Fin Aspect Ratio (FishBase)",
       y = "Pattern Aspect Ratio (A, pavo)",
       title = "Does swimming mode predict pattern orientation?",
       subtitle = "PGLS controlling for phylogeny") +
  theme_poster

print(p)
ggsave("results/recipe11-swimming-vs-pattern.pdf", p,
       width = 10, height = 8)
cat("Saved: results/recipe11-swimming-vs-pattern.pdf\n")

title: Recipe 10: Growth Rate and Color
text: Do species with faster growth rates display less chromatically conspicuous color patterns, suggesting a life history trade-off between growth and costly pigmentation?

title: Recipe 10: Growth Rate and Color
text: Do species with faster growth rates display less chromatically conspicuous color patterns, suggesting a life history trade-off between growth and costly pigmentation?

title: Recipe 10: Growth Rate and Color
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Life history trade-off



This recipe tests whether the pace of life predicts investment in costly signals. Life history theory predicts that organisms have finite energy budgets and must allocate resources among competing demands: growth, reproduction, maintenance, and defense. Conspicuous coloration can be metabolically costly to produce (carotenoid pigments, for example, must be obtained from the diet and have antioxidant functions) and ecologically costly to maintain (conspicuous individuals are more detectable to predators). If color is costly, species that invest heavily in fast growth may have less to spend on elaborate pigmentation.

title: Recipe 10: Growth Rate and Color
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
The von Bertalanffy growth coefficient (K) describes how quickly a species approaches its asymptotic body size. High K means the species grows fast and reaches adult size early; low K means slow, prolonged growth. In reef fishes, K varies enormously — from tiny cryptobenthic species that reach adult size in weeks (K > 1) to large groupers and parrotfishes that grow for decades (K < 0.1). If carotenoid or structural coloration is energetically expensive, fast growers that allocate energy primarily to somatic growth may sacrifice color investment. Alternatively, if color signals are cheap relative to growth, no trade-off will be detected, and that null result is itself informative about the cost architecture of coloration in your clade.






Clade-specific tips




Scarinae (parrotfishes): Growth rates vary substantially, from fast-growing initial-phase fish to slow-growing terminal-phase males. Since your color data likely comes from terminal-phase adults, the relevant K describes growth to that life stage.
Acanthuridae (surgeonfishes): Generally moderate growth rates with relatively conspicuous coloration. A flat relationship here might suggest that surgeon fish coloration is not particularly costly.
Any clade with high K variance: The wider the range of K values in your sample, the more power you have to detect a trade-off. Check the range before interpreting a null result.

title: Recipe 10: Growth Rate and Color
text:
The Method
We use PGLS to regress chromatic contrast (m_dS) against the von Bertalanffy growth coefficient (K) from the FishBase estimate() table. K is already on a reasonable scale (typically 0.05–2.0 for reef fishes) and does not require log transformation for most datasets. However, if your K values span several orders of magnitude, consider a log transform — inspect a histogram first.
The prediction from life history trade-off theory is a negative slope: higher K (faster growth) correlates with lower m_dS (less chromatic contrast). A positive slope would suggest that fast-growing species are actually more conspicuous, which could indicate that rapid growth enables earlier investment in signaling, or that both growth and coloration respond to the same underlying resource axis (e.g., high-quality habitat with abundant carotenoid-rich food).

title: Recipe 10: Growth Rate and Color
text:
How to Interpret Results








Result
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Negative slope, p < 0.05
Fast growers are less conspicuous
“Fast-growing species in [family] invest less in chromatic signaling, consistent with a life history trade-off between growth rate and costly coloration.”


Positive slope, p < 0.05
Fast growers are more conspicuous
“Unexpectedly, fast-growing species are more chromatically conspicuous. This may reflect shared dependence on resource-rich environments that support both rapid growth and carotenoid acquisition.”


p > 0.05
No significant relationship
“Growth rate does not predict chromatic conspicuousness in [family], suggesting that color production costs are either negligible or decoupled from somatic growth investment.”









Common pitfalls




K values in FishBase are estimates, not direct measurements for each species. Some are derived from length-frequency data, others from otolith ageing. The quality varies. Check the confidence intervals if available.
K is correlated with body size. Species with high K tend to be smaller (they reach asymptotic size quickly). This creates potential confounding with Recipe 7 (body size and complexity). Consider running Recipe 7b (size correction) to disentangle the effects.
K describes growth to asymptotic size, not juvenile growth. If color patterns change dramatically through ontogeny (e.g., pomacanthids), the K value may not correspond to the life stage at which color is expressed.

  { if (!is.null(model))
    geom_abline(intercept = coef(model)[1], slope = coef(model)[2],
                color = "#e76f51", linewidth = 1.2) } +
  labs(x = "von Bertalanffy Growth Coefficient (K)",
       y = "Mean Chromatic Contrast (m_dS)",

(2015) — Showed across ~6,000 passerine bird species that life history traits including body size significantly predict both male and female plumage coloration, after controlling for sexual selection. Demonstrates that life history trade-offs leave detectable signatures in color across large radiations. Nature, 527(7578), 367–370. DOI

These species are typically cryptically colored, consistent with the prediction that fast life histories in small-bodied species favor crypsis over costly signaling. Science, 364(6446), 1189–1192. title: Recipe 7b: Size-Corrected Color Residuals
text: Once we account for the allometric effect of body size on color patterns, does an ecological variable still predict the remaining variation in color?

title: Recipe 7b: Size-Corrected Color Residuals
text: Once we account for the allometric effect of body size on color patterns, does an ecological variable still predict the remaining variation in color?

title: Recipe 7b: Size-Corrected Color Residuals
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Residual analysis / confound removal



This recipe addresses one of the most important concepts in comparative biology: the problem of confounding variables. Body size correlates with nearly everything in ecology — depth, trophic level, growth rate, predation risk. If body size also predicts color pattern complexity (Recipe 7), then any correlation you find between an ecological variable and color might simply be a byproduct of the size–ecology association. Residual analysis removes the size effect first, then asks whether ecology explains the leftover variation. This is the comparative biology equivalent of “holding body size constant.”

title: Recipe 7b: Size-Corrected Color Residuals
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Murray’s reaction-diffusion theory (Lecture 12) tells us that body size physically constrains what patterns can form. If your clade contains species ranging from 5 cm to 100 cm, much of the variation in pattern complexity (m) might be explained by geometry alone. When you then test whether depth or diet predicts m, you might find a “significant” result that is actually driven by the fact that large fish live deeper, or that large fish are carnivores. Size correction lets you ask the more interesting question: among species of similar size, does ecology still matter?






Clade-specific tips




Scarinae (parrotfishes) and Balistoidea: These clades have the largest size ranges and therefore the greatest risk of size confounding. Size correction is essentially mandatory before interpreting any ecology–color result.
Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): With a narrow size range, size correction will remove very little variance. If your ecology result survives size correction here, it is strong evidence that the ecological effect is genuine, not an artifact of allometry.
Any clade: If the size model in step 1 is not significant (p > 0.05), there is no size effect to remove, and the residuals will be nearly identical to the raw values. That is a legitimate finding — report it!

title: Recipe 7b: Size-Corrected Color Residuals
text:
The Method
The method proceeds in three steps. First, fit a PGLS of each pavo variable against log(body size). This is the “size model” from Recipe 7. Second, extract the residuals from this model. Each residual represents how much a species deviates from the size-predicted value — it is the component of color that is not explained by body size. Positive residuals mean “more colorful/complex than expected for its size”; negative residuals mean “less than expected.” Third, test these residuals against your ecological variable of interest (e.g., depth, trophic level) using another PGLS.
The key comparison is: run your ecology analysis with raw pavo values (as in the other recipes) and then with size-corrected residuals. If the result is significant both ways, the ecological signal is robust. If it is significant with raw values but not with residuals, body size was likely driving the pattern. If it is non-significant with raw values but significant with residuals, the ecological signal was previously masked by size-related noise.

title: Recipe 7b: Size-Corrected Color Residuals
text:
How to Interpret Results








Result
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Ecology significant with raw AND residuals
Robust ecological signal independent of body size
“The relationship between [ecology] and [color metric] persists after size correction, indicating a genuine ecological effect beyond allometric scaling.”


Ecology significant with raw ONLY
Size confound likely
“The apparent relationship between [ecology] and [color metric] disappears after size correction, suggesting body size was the underlying driver.”


Ecology significant with residuals ONLY
Size was masking the signal
“After removing the allometric effect of body size, a significant relationship between [ecology] and [color metric] emerges, suggesting size variation was obscuring the ecological signal.”


Ecology non-significant both ways
No ecological signal detected
“No relationship between [ecology] and [color metric] was detected, either before or after size correction.”









Common pitfalls




Do not extract residuals from an OLS model and then use them in PGLS. The residuals must come from a PGLS model (which accounts for phylogeny) to be valid for downstream phylogenetic analysis. Using OLS residuals in PGLS can produce anti-conservative p-values.
Check that the size model is actually significant before interpreting size-corrected residuals. If size does not predict the pavo variable (p > 0.05), the residuals are essentially unchanged from the raw data, and the exercise is uninformative (though still worth reporting).
Residuals are not a magic fix for all confounds. This approach handles body size specifically. If depth and diet are correlated for reasons unrelated to size, residual analysis will not disentangle them.

title: Recipe 7b: Size-Corrected Color Residuals
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 7b: Size-Corrected Color Residuals ────────────────
source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")

# ── 1. Load your data ────────────────────────────────────────
traits <- read.csv("path/to/your/pavo_metrics.csv",
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
bundle <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")

# ── 2. Pull body size + ecology variable from FishBase ───────
# Example: testing depth after removing body size effect
fb <- pull_fishbase(traits$species,
                    fields = list(estimate = c("MaxLengthTL"),
                                  species  = c("DepthRangeDeep")))

# ── 3. Merge and filter ─────────────────────────────────────
merged <- merge(traits, fb, by = "species")
merged <- merged[!is.na(merged$MaxLengthTL) &
                  !is.na(merged$DepthRangeDeep) &
                  merged$MaxLengthTL > 0 &
                  merged$DepthRangeDeep > 0, ]
merged$log_size  <- log(merged$MaxLengthTL)
merged$log_depth <- log(merged$DepthRangeDeep)

cat("Species with both size and depth data:", nrow(merged), "\n")

# ── 4. Match to tree ────────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, merged, species_col = "species")

# ── 5. Step 1: Fit size models and extract residuals ─────────
pavo_vars <- c("m", "Jc", "m_dS")   # adjust as needed

for (v in pavo_vars) {
  cat("\n── Size correction for", v, "──\n")

  # Fit PGLS: pavo ~ log(size)
  f_size <- as.formula(paste(v, "~ log_size"))
  size_model <- safe_pgls(f_size, df = matched$data, tree = matched$tree)

  if (!is.null(size_model)) {
    # Extract residuals (these are phylogenetically-informed residuals)
    resid_col <- paste0(v, "_resid")
    matched$data[[resid_col]] <- residuals(size_model)
  }
}

# ── 6. Step 2: Test residuals against ecology variable ───────
cat("\n── Testing size-corrected residuals vs depth ──\n")

# Raw model (for comparison)
model_raw <- safe_pgls(m_dS ~ log_depth, df = matched$data,
                        tree = matched$tree)

# Size-corrected model
model_resid <- safe_pgls(m_dS_resid ~ log_depth, df = matched$data,
                          tree = matched$tree)

# ── 7. Comparison plot ──────────────────────────────────────
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # for side-by-side panels

p_raw <- ggplot(matched$data, aes(x = log_depth, y = m_dS)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.7, color = "#264653") +
  { if (!is.null(model_raw))
    geom_abline(intercept = coef(model_raw)[1], slope = coef(model_raw)[2],
                color = "#e76f51", linewidth = 1.2) } +
  labs(x = "log(Depth)", y = "Chromatic Contrast (m_dS)",
       title = "Raw values") +
  theme_poster

p_resid <- ggplot(matched$data, aes(x = log_depth, y = m_dS_resid)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.7, color = "#2a9d8f") +
  { if (!is.null(model_resid))
    geom_abline(intercept = coef(model_resid)[1],
                slope = coef(model_resid)[2],
                color = "#e76f51", linewidth = 1.2) } +
  labs(x = "log(Depth)", y = "Size-Corrected Residuals (m_dS)",
       title = "After size correction") +
  theme_poster

combo <- p_raw + p_resid +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Does depth predict chromatic contrast before and after size correction?",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 24, face = "bold"))
  )

print(combo)
ggsave("results/recipe7b-size-correction-comparison.pdf", combo,
       width = 18, height = 8)
cat("Saved: results/recipe7b-size-correction-comparison.pdf\n")

title: Recipe 7b: Size-Corrected Color Residuals
text:
From the Literature

Murray, J. D. (1981) — Established the theoretical basis for why body size constrains pattern complexity: the surface area available for reaction-diffusion dynamics determines which spatial modes are stable. This is the primary motivation for size correction in color pattern analyses. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 295(1078), 473–496. DOI


Dale, J., Dey, C. J., Delhey, K., Kempenaers, B., & Valcu, M. (2015) — Quantified plumage coloration across ~6,000 passerine species and showed that body size is a significant predictor of ornamentation in both sexes, even after controlling for sexual selection and life history. Demonstrates the importance of accounting for allometric effects in comparative analyses of coloration. Nature, 527(7578), 367–370. DOI

title: Recipe 15: Discrete Trait Mapping
text: Does the presence of bars, spots, or stripes map onto the phylogeny in a structured way — or did the same pattern evolve independently many times?

title: Recipe 15: Discrete Trait Mapping
text: Does the presence of bars, spots, or stripes map onto the phylogeny in a structured way — or did the same pattern evolve independently many times?

title: Recipe 15: Discrete Trait Mapping
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Ancestral State Reconstruction / Character Evolution



You are treating a pattern type (bars present / absent, spots present / absent) as a discrete character and asking whether it evolved once and was retained, or evolved repeatedly. The core method is ancestral state reconstruction (ASR) — estimating the most probable state at each internal node of the phylogeny given the observed tip states.
This is the same logic that evolutionary biologists use to infer when flight was lost in birds, when viviparity evolved in lizards, or when C4 photosynthesis arose in grasses. Here, your character is a visible color pattern element that you score yourself from images.

title: Recipe 15: Discrete Trait Mapping
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Discrete trait mapping answers a question that pavo metrics alone cannot: did a recognizable pattern type arise once and diversify, or is it a convergent solution appearing over and over?






Natural fits for this recipe




Balistoidea — Triggerfishes span plain, spotted, striped, and boldly barred forms. Did bold bars arise once in the triggerfishes or multiple times across the group?
Pomacanthidae — Many angelfishes shift dramatically from juvenile to adult pattern. Score adults only, and ask whether bold vertical banding is ancestral or repeatedly derived.
Scarinae — Terminal-phase males often carry bold stripes and spots. Did these elements track phylogeny or reflect repeated convergence?
Acanthuridae — The contrast between the plain-bodied Naso unicornfishes and the patterned surgeonfish core is stark. When did plain coloration evolve in the group?
Any clade — Pick whichever binary trait (bars, spots, eyespots, ocelli, etc.) varies across your species and has a clear visual definition you can apply consistently from images.



The pattern of gains and losses tells you about selective pressure. A single origin that persists (low rate of change) suggests strong stabilizing selection or functional constraint. Many independent gains suggest that the same selection pressure recurs in different lineages.

title: Recipe 15: Discrete Trait Mapping
text:
The Method
Step 1 — Define your trait precisely. Before touching any code, write a one-sentence definition of what you are scoring. For bars: “a bar is a vertical dark stripe at least as wide as one eye diameter that crosses more than half the body depth.” This level of precision lets a second person score the same images and get the same answer.
Step 2 — Score your images. Go through each species in your image set (the same images you used for pavo). Record a 1 if the trait is present, 0 if absent, and NA if the image quality is too low to judge. Put the result in a two-column CSV: species, has_bars (or whatever you named the trait).
Step 3 — Match to the tree. Keep only the species that appear in both your CSV and your mini-tree. Drop tips for which you have no score.
Step 4 — Plot trait on tips. Color tree tips by trait state (two colors from the course palette). This visual inspection alone is informative — if one color is clustered in one part of the tree, structure exists.
Step 5 — Run ancestral state reconstruction. Use ace() from the ape package with type = "discrete" and model = "ER" (equal-rates: a single rate parameter governs gains and losses). This is the most conservative assumption. The function returns, for each internal node, the estimated probability of being in each state.
Step 6 — Plot pie charts on nodes. Each internal node gets a pie chart showing P(absent) and P(bars). Nodes with mixed probabilities (roughly 50/50) are genuinely uncertain — that is honest. Nodes with one color dominant are informative.
Step 7 — Count transitions. Use phytools::make.simmap() (optional, see code below) to stochastically map transitions. Summarizing 100 maps gives you a distribution over the number of gains and losses, which is more honest than a single reconstruction.

title: Recipe 15: Discrete Trait Mapping
text:
How to Interpret Results







What you see
What it means




Trait tips cluster in one clade
Single origin (or a single origin plus a few losses). The pattern is phylogenetically structured.


Trait tips scattered across the whole tree
Many independent gains, many losses, or both. Low phylogenetic signal in this binary trait.


Root node pie is mostly one color
The ancestral state is probably resolved. The other state is derived.


Root node pie is 50/50
The ancestral state cannot be resolved with your data — both scenarios are equally supported.


High rate parameter (printed by ace)
Trait is labile; changes frequently relative to branch lengths.


Low rate parameter
Trait is conserved; once present, it persists.



Pitfalls to avoid:

Inconsistent scoring is fatal. If “bars present” means different things for different species, your reconstruction will be garbage. Score all species in one sitting using your written definition.
NA vs. 0 matters. An unscored species is not the same as an absent trait. Drop NAs before running ace().
Equal-rates is a simplification. Gains and losses need not occur at the same rate. After you get the basic result, you can compare ER to ARD (all-rates-different) with AIC(). But ER is appropriate for an undergraduate project.
Tree uncertainty. You are using a point-estimate tree. The reconstruction could differ on an alternative topology. Mention this as a caveat.

title: Recipe 15: Discrete Trait Mapping
text:
The Code

library(ape)
library(phytools)

source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")

# ── Load your tree ────────────────────────────────────────────────
bundle <- load_bundle("path/to/your/bundle")
tree   <- bundle$tree

# ── Load your scored trait CSV ────────────────────────────────────
# Create this file yourself from visual inspection of your images.
# Two columns: species (underscore format, e.g. Balistes_vetula), has_bars (0 or 1)
scored <- read.csv("my_bar_scores.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Remove rows with NA scores
scored <- scored[!is.na(scored$has_bars), ]

# Named vector: values are 0/1, names are species
bars <- setNames(scored$has_bars, scored$species)

# ── Prune tree to scored species ──────────────────────────────────
overlap     <- intersect(names(bars), tree$tip.label)
tree_pruned <- drop.tip(tree, setdiff(tree$tip.label, overlap))
bars        <- bars[tree_pruned$tip.label]

cat("Scored species in tree:", length(overlap), "\n")
cat("Trait prevalence: n =", sum(bars), "with trait,",
    sum(bars == 0), "without\n")

# ── Plot tips colored by trait state ──────────────────────────────
cols <- c("0" = "#2a9d8f", "1" = "#e76f51")

png("fig-trait-tips.png", width = 2400, height = 2000, res = 300)
plot(tree_pruned,
     type      = "fan",
     cex       = 0.45,
     edge.width = 2.5,
     tip.color = cols[as.character(bars)])
legend("topleft",
       legend = c("No bars", "Bars"),
       fill   = c("#2a9d8f", "#e76f51"),
       cex    = 1.2,
       bty    = "n")
title("Trait distribution: bars")
dev.off()

# ── Ancestral state reconstruction ────────────────────────────────
anc <- ace(as.factor(bars), tree_pruned, type = "discrete", model = "ER")

cat("\nTransition rate (equal-rates model):\n")
cat("  q =", round(anc$rates, 4), "\n")

cat("\nAncestral state at root:\n")
cat("  P(no bars) =", round(anc$lik.anc[1, 1], 3), "\n")
cat("  P(bars)    =", round(anc$lik.anc[1, 2], 3), "\n")

# ── Plot reconstruction with pie charts on nodes ──────────────────
png("fig-ancestral-state.png", width = 2400, height = 2000, res = 300)
plot(tree_pruned,
     type       = "fan",
     cex        = 0.40,
     edge.width = 2)
nodelabels(pie    = anc$lik.anc,
           piecol = c("#2a9d8f", "#e76f51"),
           cex    = 0.40)
legend("topleft",
       legend = c("No bars", "Bars"),
       fill   = c("#2a9d8f", "#e76f51"),
       cex    = 1.2,
       bty    = "n")
title("Ancestral state reconstruction: bars")
dev.off()

# ── Optional: Stochastic character mapping ────────────────────────
# This gives a distribution over the number of transitions rather
# than a single point estimate. Run 100 simulations and summarize.
set.seed(42)
maps   <- make.simmap(tree_pruned, as.factor(bars), model = "ER", nsim = 100,
                      message = FALSE)
map_summary <- describe.simmap(maps)

cat("\nStochastic mapping summary (100 simulations):\n")
cat("  Mean transitions (0 -> 1):", round(mean(map_summary$count[, "0,1"]), 1), "\n")
cat("  Mean transitions (1 -> 0):", round(mean(map_summary$count[, "1,0"]), 1), "\n")

# Plot the summary map
png("fig-simmap.png", width = 2400, height = 2000, res = 300)
plot(map_summary,
     type   = "fan",
     fsize  = 0.40,
     colors = c("0" = "#2a9d8f", "1" = "#e76f51"),
     lwd    = 2)
add.simmap.legend(colors = c("0" = "#2a9d8f", "1" = "#e76f51"),
                  x      = 0, y = 0,
                  prompt = FALSE,
                  fsize  = 1.0)
title("Stochastic character mapping: bars")
dev.off()

What to report on your poster:

The tip-colored tree (fast visual check for clustering)
The pie-chart reconstruction (your main result)
The root-state probabilities (P(absent) vs. P(bars))
The estimated number of transitions from the stochastic mapping
A one-sentence interpretation: “Bars appear to have evolved [once / twice / multiple times] in this family, with [high / low] probability that the ancestor was [barred / unbarred].”

title: Recipe 15: Discrete Trait Mapping
text:
From the Literature
Pagel, M. (1994). Detecting correlated evolution on phylogenies: a general method for the comparative analysis of discrete characters. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 255, 37–45. The foundational paper for comparing discrete character evolution across phylogenies. Introduces the likelihood framework that underlies ace(). Read the methods section to understand why equal-rates versus all-rates-different models exist and what the log-likelihood ratio test measures.
Schluter, D., Price, T., Mooers, A. O., & Ludwig, D. (1997). Likelihood of ancestor states in adaptive radiation. Evolution, 51, 1699–1711. Establishes the connection between ancestral state reconstruction and inference about adaptive origins. Explains when ancestral state reconstruction is reliable (many taxa, short branches near the root) and when it is not (long branches, few taxa, fast-evolving trait).
Revell, L. J. (2012). phytools: an R package for phylogenetic comparative biology (and other things). Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 3, 217–223. Documents the make.simmap() function used in the stochastic mapping extension above. If you use the simmap output in your poster, cite this paper.

title: Project Milestone Checklist
text:
Reference: Hypothesis vs. Description
Writing a hypothesis-driven result is different from simply reporting a number. Compare these examples:


Less effective (description only):
“We found K = 0.32 for transition density in pomacanthids.”
“The phyloPCA shows that species cluster by genus.”
“PGLS gave p = 0.07.”
These report numbers without framing, prediction, or interpretation.



More effective (hypothesis-driven):
“If color pattern complexity tracks ecology, we predict significant PGLS and K near 1. We found K = 0.32 (p = 0.04) and non-significant PGLS (p = 0.41), consistent with the butterflyfish decoupling pattern.”
“The phyloPCA separates angelfishes along a conspicuousness axis (PC1: m_dS loading = -1.00), suggesting that chromatic boundary strength — not stripe frequency — is the primary dimension of color diversification.”
These state predictions, report evidence, and interpret results in context.

Variable
Full name
What it captures
